The listener should therefore point out the error privately and discreetly, perhaps after the meeting or in a one-on-one conversation. This approach corrects the mistake while preserving the colleague's dignity and maintaining a harmonious working relationship. Publicly criticising the proposal would likely cause the colleague to lose face, which is something people in China generally try to avoid.

In France, sitting with legs spread apart and slouched is not the usual expectation at a formal dinner. The common practice is to sit upright with legs together and feet flat on the floor. This posture is seen as a sign of good manners and respect for the occasion and the other guests. Therefore, the person should sit upright with legs together and feet flat on the floor. Sitting with legs spread apart and slouched would likely be viewed as careless or disrespectful in this setting.

In Hungary, when two women meet for the first time in a business setting, it is common to greet each other with a kiss on the cheek. This practice is a friendly and warm way to acknowledge the other person, even in professional contexts. Therefore, they should greet each other with a kiss on the cheek. A handshake would feel too formal and distant for this situation, as the kiss is the expected and accepted greeting between women in Hungary.

In Hungary, dropping by a friend's home on a weekday afternoon without prior arrangement is not the usual expectation. People there generally prefer to arrange visits in advance, so the person should contact the friend beforehand to agree on a time. This allows the friend to be prepared and shows consideration for their schedule. The person should therefore call or message the friend to arrange the visit before going over.

In Ireland, avoiding eye contact when greeting someone is not the usual practice. People there generally make eye contact while greeting a new colleague. So in this hallway meeting, the person should look the colleague in the eye. This shows engagement and respect, which is what is expected in such a first encounter. Avoiding eye contact could come across as shyness or disinterest, which is not the impression one wants to give.

In Ireland, a bow is not the usual way for colleagues to greet each other when they meet for the first time in a business setting. The common expectation is a handshake, which is a straightforward and friendly way to acknowledge the other person. So in this situation, the two colleagues would most likely shake hands. A bow would be unusual and might seem overly formal or out of place in an Irish business context.

In Iraq, the idea that men are not expected to stand to greet a woman when she enters the room is not accurate. The common expectation is that a man should rise from his seat when a woman enters, as a sign of respect. Therefore, in this situation, the man should stand up when the woman enters the room. Remaining seated would likely be seen as disrespectful or dismissive. Standing is a customary way to acknowledge her presence and show courtesy.

In Italy, using a first name right away is not the usual way to show friendliness in a first meeting with a manager. Avoiding offense or disruption in interpersonal interactions matters, so people tend to be more formal at the start. The common expectation is to address the manager by their title and surname until they invite you to use their first name. Therefore, the employee should use the manager's title and surname. This approach respects the professional relationship and avoids any awkwardness that could come from presuming familiarity.

In Italy, delivering sensitive news bluntly is not the usual expectation. Avoiding offense or disruption to another person matters, so the manager should soften the message. The manager should explain that the proposal was not approved while acknowledging its strengths. This approach respects the employee's effort and maintains a good working relationship. Simply stating that the proposal was not approved without any positive acknowledgment would likely feel harsh and dismissive.

In Italy, the idea that younger people typically enter a room first is not the usual expectation. Avoiding offense or disruption to others is important, so the elderly are given precedence. The common practice is for the elderly to enter a room first, followed by younger people. Therefore, in this situation, the elderly relative should enter the room first. This shows respect for their age and position within the family.

In Kenya, skipping or rushing the greeting is not acceptable; it is seen as rude. The businessperson should therefore take the time to greet the colleague properly before starting the meeting. A quick hello without a proper greeting would likely be perceived as disrespectful. Taking a moment to acknowledge the colleague shows consideration and helps establish a positive working relationship.

In Cambodia, a businesswoman is not typically addressed by her first name in a business setting. The common expectation is to use her title and surname, which shows respect and maintains a professional distance. Therefore, the client should address her by her title and surname. Using her first name would be too informal and could be seen as disrespectful in this context.

In Laos, pointing with the index finger is not the usual way to indicate direction. The common expectation is to use an open hand, with the palm facing up or outward, to gesture toward the place. So when a visitor asks for directions to the nearest market, the resident should point with an open hand rather than a single finger. This approach is considered more polite and appropriate in everyday interactions. Using an index finger could come across as abrupt or impolite, even if no offense is intended. Therefore, the resident should use an open hand to show the visitor the way.

In Lebanon, receiving a gift with the left hand only is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to accept a gift with the right hand or with both hands. This shows respect and appreciation for the gesture. Therefore, the coworker should receive the gift with the right hand or both hands. Using the left hand alone would be seen as less polite in this context.

In Malta, the idea that the couple themselves generally pay for the wedding expenses is not the usual expectation. Supporting the welfare of close family members is important, and this often means that the families of the bride and groom share the cost of the wedding. The couple's families typically contribute to the wedding expenses, and this is a common practice rather than an exception. Therefore, in this situation, the couple's families should pay for the wedding expenses, as it reflects the caring and supportive role that families play in such celebrations.

In Malta, dropping by someone's home without prior arrangement is not the usual expectation. People there generally prefer to know in advance when a visitor is coming. The person should contact the friend beforehand to arrange the visit. This gives the friend time to prepare and shows consideration for their schedule. Simply showing up unannounced could be seen as intrusive or inconvenient.

In Nepal, sexually suggestive jokes are not something people generally tell in a workplace break. The expectation is to avoid such jokes, as they are not considered appropriate in that setting. So the person should refrain from telling the joke. Telling it would go against the common preference for keeping humor clean and respectful in a professional environment.

In Nepal, a direct 'no' is not seen as clear, honest, and respectful; it can come across as abrupt or even rude. People there generally prefer to soften a refusal or avoid a blunt negative. So when a colleague asks if you can take on an extra task, you should respond in a way that is indirect, such as saying you will see what you can do or that you will try to help. This approach preserves the relationship and shows consideration for the other person's feelings. A straightforward 'no' would likely be perceived as too harsh and could damage the working relationship.

In Pakistan, the left hand is not the usual choice for shaking hands. The common expectation is to use the right hand when greeting someone, especially in a workplace setting. So when this man meets his new colleague, he should offer his right hand. Using the left hand could be seen as inappropriate or disrespectful in this context. The right hand is the standard for greetings and handshakes there.

In Peru, a guest is not expected to greet only the host upon entering a small gathering. The common expectation is to greet everyone present, including the host and any other acquaintances. This practice reflects a general courtesy of acknowledging each person individually rather than singling out the host. Therefore, the person should greet everyone present, including the host and any other acquaintances. Greeting only the host would likely be seen as overlooking the others and would not fit the usual social expectation in Peru.

In the Philippines, a neutral expression is not the usual expectation when meeting someone for the first time. People there generally smile when they greet others, as a smile is seen as a sign of friendliness and openness. So when introduced to a new colleague, the person should smile. This helps create a warm and welcoming atmosphere, which is common in Filipino social interactions. A neutral expression might come across as cold or distant in this context.

In Papua New Guinea, a slight bow without physical contact is not the usual way to greet an acquaintance on the street. The common expectation is to shake hands, which is a customary greeting in this setting. Therefore, the person should shake hands with the acquaintance. Bowing without touching would not fit the customary practice there.

In Serbia, the elderly are not treated as ordinary passengers; they are given special respect. On a crowded bus, a young person is expected to notice an elderly passenger boarding and standing nearby. The appropriate action is to offer the seat to the elderly passenger. Remaining seated would be seen as failing to show the respect that is commonly expected toward older people in this setting.

In Serbia, a gentle handshake with averted eyes is not the usual way colleagues greet each other at a business meeting. The common expectation is a firm handshake accompanied by direct eye contact. This conveys confidence and sincerity, which are important in professional interactions. Therefore, the two colleagues should greet each other with a firm handshake and direct eye contact. A gentle handshake with averted eyes might be seen as lacking engagement or confidence.

In Syria, praise is not usually reserved for exceptional achievements. People there commonly express appreciation for routine tasks as well, because acknowledging a colleague's effort is important. So when a colleague finishes a routine task, coworkers would most likely offer praise for the work itself. This fits the situation because the task is completed, and the coworkers want to show that they value the colleague's contribution. Waiting for an exceptional achievement would miss the chance to recognize the work that was just done.

In Timor-Leste, a host is not expected to leave a guest without any refreshments during a short visit. The usual practice is to offer something to drink, such as water, tea, or coffee, and often a snack like fruit or biscuits. This is a common way of welcoming someone into the home and showing care. So in this situation, the host would typically offer the guest a drink and a snack. Not offering anything would feel less hospitable and less in line with what is generally expected.

In Tonga, a quick lifting of the eyebrows is commonly understood as a nonverbal way of saying “no.” This gesture serves as a brief, silent refusal or negative response. When a colleague asks a question and the person quickly lifts their eyebrows, it indicates that they are declining or disagreeing with the question. The movement is a recognized signal in Tongan communication, even without any spoken words. Therefore, the eyebrow movement indicates “no” rather than “yes.”

In Tonga, a brief nod is not the usual way acquaintances greet each other on the street. The common greeting is a kiss on the cheek, which is a warm and friendly gesture between people who know each other. So when two acquaintances meet, they would most likely exchange a kiss on the cheek rather than just a nod. This fits the situation because it is the expected way to acknowledge someone in a casual, everyday encounter. A nod would feel too formal or distant for this kind of interaction.

In Türkiye, the idea that peers are approached first during greetings is not the usual expectation. Avoiding offense or disruption toward others is important, so greetings are directed toward the oldest person present. The young adult should therefore greet the older relative first. Greeting the peer first would overlook the older relative and could be seen as disrespectful.

In Türkiye, gift wrapping and cards are common, so a birthday present for a close friend would typically be presented in a nicely wrapped box with a card. The person would most likely take the time to wrap the gift neatly and include a card with a personal message. Giving the gift without wrapping or a card would feel less thoughtful and less in keeping with the usual practice. Therefore, the person would present the gift in a nicely wrapped box with a card.

In the United States, a neutral expression during a greeting is not the usual expectation. People generally try to appear friendly and approachable when they meet someone, so a smile is common and expected. The person should smile while greeting the acquaintance. A neutral expression might come across as cold or uninterested, which is not the impression most people want to give in this setting.

In Vietnam, white is not typically associated with purity and is not a common choice for festive occasions like weddings. Instead, white is strongly linked to mourning and funerals, so wearing a white dress to a wedding would be seen as inappropriate and could cause offense. The woman should therefore choose a dress in a color other than white, such as red, yellow, or another bright hue, to align with the festive and joyful nature of the event. This choice shows respect for local customs and avoids any unintended association with mourning.

In Samoa, a serious and reserved demeanor is not the usual expectation between coworkers during a break. People there generally prefer to be relaxed and open, so it is common for coworkers to chat casually and share jokes. In this office kitchen setting, the customary thing would be for them to talk informally and laugh together. Keeping the conversation serious and avoiding humor would feel out of place for many Samoans.

In Zimbabwe, a woman speaking with a male colleague in a hallway is not expected to maintain direct eye contact. The common expectation is that women avoid direct eye contact with men. Therefore, she should avoid direct eye contact with the male colleague during the conversation. This approach aligns with the local practice of not looking directly at a man while speaking with him.

In Argentina, pointing with the index finger is not considered acceptable; it is generally seen as rude. The visitor should avoid using the index finger to gesture to the server. Instead, a more polite way to get the server's attention is to raise a hand slightly or make eye contact and nod. This approach is more respectful and aligns with common expectations in Argentine restaurants. Using the index finger could be perceived as impolite or aggressive, so it is best to avoid it.

In Argentina, the idea that relatives are not expected to visit frequently when they live nearby is not accurate. Maintaining close relationships with family members is important there, and this is reflected in how often people visit each other. When relatives live in the same neighborhood, it is common and expected for them to see each other often. Therefore, the person should visit their cousin frequently, as this shows care and keeps the family bond strong. Not visiting often would go against the expectation of staying connected with close family members.

In Germany, close friends do not typically greet each other with a handshake. The common expectation among close friends is to hug and kiss each other on the cheek. So when these two friends meet after a week apart, they should hug and kiss each other on the cheek. A handshake would feel too formal and distant for such a close relationship.

In Germany, entering a room without knocking when the door is closed is not the usual expectation. Avoiding disruption or offense to others matters, so people generally knock before opening a closed door. The colleague should knock on the door before opening it. This shows consideration for whoever is inside and respects their privacy. Simply opening the door without knocking could be seen as intrusive or rude.

In Germany, a colleague asking for feedback on a draft report is not expecting a tactful, indirect answer. The usual expectation is to give a direct, honest answer to a question. So the team member should tell the colleague exactly what they think of the draft report, without softening the message. This directness is seen as a sign of respect for the other person's need for clear information. Giving a tactful, indirect answer would likely be read as evasive or unhelpful.

In Egypt, close friends and family do not usually keep their distance during conversations. Physical contact is a common part of everyday interaction between people who are close. So in this café setting, the two friends would likely touch each other often, such as by patting each other's arm or shoulder, or by holding hands. This kind of touch is a natural expression of their friendship, not an unusual or intrusive gesture. The idea that they would rarely touch each other does not reflect the usual pattern of closeness in Egyptian social life.

In Egypt, strict punctuality is not the usual expectation for business meetings. It is common for people to arrive late, and this is generally accepted as part of the business culture. Therefore, the customary approach is to arrive late. Arriving on time would not align with the common practice in this context.

In Ethiopia, a direct apology by saying "I am sorry" is not the usual way to handle an accidental foot-step. People there often prefer to show remorse through a gesture rather than words. The common expectation is to touch the other person's hand or arm to express regret. So in this crowded market, the person should gently touch the other person's hand or arm. This non-verbal gesture fits the situation because it acknowledges the mistake without the need for explicit verbal apology.

In Ethiopia, pointing directly at a person is not the usual way to indicate someone. The common expectation is to avoid pointing at a person directly. Instead, the visitor should gesture toward the person without pointing. This approach is more appropriate in this situation.

In Ethiopia, female sexual modesty is considered especially important, so the claim that it is not is incorrect. At a community gathering, a young woman is expected to dress in a way that covers her body modestly. This means choosing clothing that is not tight or revealing, and that provides adequate coverage. Wearing something that is tight or revealing would go against the common expectation of modesty in this setting. Therefore, she should wear clothing that covers her body modestly.

In Indonesia, keeping shoes on when entering a mosque is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to remove shoes before stepping inside a place of worship. For a visitor about to enter a mosque for a tour, this means taking off their shoes at the entrance. Doing so shows respect for the sacred space and aligns with local customs. Keeping shoes on would be seen as disregarding the customary practice.

In Indonesia, receiving a business card with the left hand only is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to receive the card with both hands or with the right hand only. This shows respect and attentiveness to the person offering the card. Using the left hand alone can be seen as careless or disrespectful in this context. Therefore, you should receive the card with both hands or with the right hand only.

In Indonesia, the idea that flowers are not typically given on special occasions like weddings is not accurate. Flowers are commonly given on special occasions such as marriages and funerals. For a wedding ceremony, the colleague should bring flowers. This is a customary and appreciated gesture in Indonesian wedding celebrations. Bringing flowers fits the expectation for such events, whereas not bringing them might seem less thoughtful in this context.

In Indonesia, the idea that people generally avoid asking about marital status to respect privacy is not accurate. It is common for relatives to ask a single adult about their marital status, and this is not usually seen as an intrusion. At a family gathering, the single adult can expect to be asked about their relationship plans or whether they are seeing someone. The question is a normal part of conversation among relatives, not a breach of privacy. Therefore, the single adult should anticipate being asked about their marital status during the conversation.

In India, a guest is not expected to decline what is offered, especially chai. Accepting the offer is a way of showing respect and appreciation for the host's hospitality. Therefore, the guest should accept the cup of chai. Politely declining could be seen as rejecting the host's kindness and may cause discomfort.

In Japan, receiving a gift with one hand is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to accept a gift with both hands, as this shows respect and appreciation for the giver. Therefore, the coworker should receive the gift with both hands. This approach aligns with the polite and considerate manner expected in Japanese workplace interactions.

In Japan, there is a common expectation that one does not refill another person's cup without being asked. This practice reflects a consideration for the other person's preferences and a reluctance to impose. In a business meeting, a colleague's empty teacup should therefore be left as it is, and the colleague should be given the opportunity to request a refill. Refilling the cup without being asked could be seen as presumptuous or intrusive. The appropriate action is to wait for the colleague to indicate that they would like more tea.

In Japan, counting change in front of a cashier is not the usual expectation. It is generally seen as impolite to count the money while the cashier is still there. The customer should therefore accept the change without counting it in front of the cashier. This shows consideration for the cashier and avoids drawing attention to the transaction. Counting the change in front of the cashier would be considered rude.

In Japan, a direct and blunt response is not the usual expectation when someone asks about a proposed timeline. People there generally prefer to avoid causing offense or disruption, so they tend to soften their answers. The team member should therefore say that the timeline may not be realistic, rather than stating it bluntly. This phrasing allows the colleague to understand the concern without feeling confronted. A blunt statement could be seen as too harsh or disrespectful in a team setting.

In Japan, arriving late to a scheduled meeting is not the usual expectation. Punctuality is important, and people generally try to be on time for appointments. The person should arrive at the scheduled time. Being late could be seen as disrespectful or careless, so it is better to make an effort to be there when the meeting is set to begin.

In Japan, answering or using a mobile phone during a business meeting is not considered acceptable. The expectation is to keep the phone silent and avoid using it while the meeting is in progress. Therefore, the participant should silence the phone and ignore the call. This shows respect for the meeting and the other participants. Answering the call would be seen as disruptive and unprofessional.

In Japan, chewing with one’s mouth open is not considered acceptable; it is generally seen as rude. The expectation is to keep one’s mouth closed while eating. Therefore, the person should chew with their mouth closed while eating lunch with the colleague. This shows consideration for the other person and aligns with common dining etiquette in Japan.

In Russia, there is a common belief that breaking a mirror brings bad luck. To prevent this misfortune, people often knock on wood three times. This practice is a way to ward off the negative consequences associated with the broken mirror. Therefore, the person should knock on wood three times after breaking the mirror. Doing so is thought to neutralize the bad luck and restore good fortune.

In Russia, arranging a meeting at short notice is not the usual expectation. People there generally prefer to schedule appointments in advance, giving the other person time to prepare and showing consideration for their schedule. The manager should therefore contact the colleague well ahead of time to arrange the meeting. This approach fits the situation because it respects the colleague's time and allows for proper planning of the project update discussion.

In Russia, the idea that men are not expected to open doors for women is not accurate. It is a common courtesy for a man to open a door for a woman when they are approaching an entrance at the same time. This expectation reflects a traditional sense of politeness and respect in everyday interactions. Therefore, in this situation, the man should open the door for the woman. Not doing so would be seen as lacking in basic courtesy.

In Chile, avoiding direct eye contact is not the usual expectation when greeting someone. On the contrary, direct eye contact is important when greeting someone. Therefore, when meeting a new colleague for the first time in a hallway, the person should make direct eye contact while greeting the colleague. This shows engagement and respect in the interaction. Avoiding eye contact might be seen as evasive or unfriendly in this context.

In Chile, taking more food than one can eat is not considered acceptable; it is generally seen as wasteful and disrespectful to the host. Avoiding waste and showing consideration for others are important, so guests are expected to take only what they can finish. At a buffet dinner party, the guest should therefore serve themselves a modest amount of food that they are sure to eat. This shows respect for the host's effort and the food provided, and it prevents unnecessary leftovers. Taking a large portion that might go uneaten would go against this common expectation.

In Cyprus, older women commonly prefer to meet in public settings such as cafes or parks rather than in private homes. This preference reflects a social expectation that gatherings among older women are often arranged in open, accessible places. For two older women planning a social visit, a cafe or park would be the most likely choice. Meeting at one of their homes would be less typical, as public venues are generally favored for such social interactions.

In Spain, entering a shop without greeting anyone is not the usual expectation. People generally expect a customer to acknowledge the staff when they come in. A simple 'hola' or 'buenos días' is enough to show politeness. So in this bakery, the customer should greet the staff upon entering. This fits the situation because the customer is walking into a small bakery and looking at the display, which means they are in a place where a greeting is expected.

In rural Fiji, it is not the case that people remain silent when passing others. On the contrary, it is common to exchange a greeting as a sign of respect and friendliness. Therefore, the person should greet the other person when passing them. This practice reflects a general expectation of acknowledging others in rural settings. Remaining silent would be seen as unfriendly or dismissive.

In the United Kingdom, a birthday gift is not usually expected to be of high monetary value. The common expectation is that the gift should be modest in price. Therefore, the colleague should choose a modest gift. A high-value gift could be seen as excessive or inappropriate for a coworker relationship.

In Hong Kong, giving sharp objects like knives or scissors as a housewarming gift is not a good idea. These items are commonly associated with cutting ties or severing relationships, so they carry a negative meaning in this context. For a friend's housewarming, it is better to choose something that does not suggest ending a connection. A safer and more appropriate gift would be something other than a sharp object, such as a plant or a decorative item for the home. This way, the gift expresses good wishes without any unintended implication of severing the friendship.

In Hong Kong, giving or receiving an item with one hand is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to use both hands when accepting something from another person. This shows respect and attentiveness in a professional setting. Therefore, the receiving colleague should accept the document with both hands. Using one hand might be seen as careless or disrespectful.

In Hong Kong, the idea that children should maintain a balanced life without excessive focus on academic excellence does not reflect the common expectation. Academic achievement is highly valued, and children are generally expected to strive for excellence in their studies. When a child comes home with average grades, the appropriate response is to focus on improving those grades. This means putting effort into studying, seeking help when needed, and treating schoolwork as a serious priority. A balanced life that de-emphasizes academic performance would likely be seen as not meeting the expected standard. Therefore, the child should concentrate on raising their grades rather than on other activities.

In Croatia, a large gift basket is not something to keep for oneself. The common expectation is to share it with others, so the person should open the basket and offer its contents to colleagues or friends. This shows appreciation for the gift and avoids the impression of being self-centered. Keeping the basket entirely for oneself would go against the spirit of generosity that is valued in such situations.

In Hungary, a meeting is not typically opened by jumping straight into business matters. It is common to begin with a few minutes of personal small talk, allowing everyone to connect before turning to the agenda. The team leader should therefore start with some light conversation, such as asking how everyone is or commenting on something general, and only then move on to the quarterly results. This approach fits the expectation that meetings begin with a brief personal exchange rather than a direct focus on work.

In Ireland, public displays of emotion, affection, or attachment are not uncommon and are generally accepted. At a train station, it would be customary for a couple to kiss and hug when saying goodbye. This kind of physical affection is seen as a normal expression of care and closeness, not something to be avoided. Therefore, the couple would likely embrace and kiss before parting, rather than keeping their distance.

In Ireland, it is common for men to greet both male and female friends with a kiss on the cheek. This is a warm and friendly way to show affection in social settings. When meeting his friends at a social gathering, the man should therefore kiss both his male and female friends on the cheek. A handshake would feel too formal and distant for such a casual encounter. The cheek kiss is the expected and appropriate greeting in this situation.

In Iran, openly celebrating and taking pride in one's success is not the usual expectation. Humility is valued, and people are expected to limit self-importance and avoid status display. When others congratulate the colleague on the promotion, the colleague should respond with modesty, downplaying the achievement and attributing the success to others. This approach fits the situation because it shows humility and avoids drawing attention to oneself. Openly celebrating and taking pride in the promotion would go against the expectation of limiting self-importance.

In Cambodia, the left hand is not the usual choice for passing or receiving items. The common expectation is to use the right hand for such exchanges. Therefore, the person should use the right hand to pass the document to the colleague. Using the left hand would not fit this preference and could be seen as inappropriate in this situation.

In South Korea, using the left hand alone to offer or receive something is not appropriate. The common expectation is to use the right hand or both hands when giving or taking an item. Therefore, the colleague should offer the document using the right hand or both hands. This practice shows consideration for the other person and aligns with local customs. Offering with the left hand alone would be seen as disrespectful or careless.

In Laos, direct eye contact is not expected to be held continuously without diverting the gaze. The common practice is to divert the gaze from time to time while speaking. This allows the person to maintain eye contact without staring, which can feel too intense or confrontational. Therefore, the person should divert their gaze from time to time while speaking with the colleague. Maintaining direct eye contact continuously would not fit this expectation and could make the interaction feel uncomfortable.

In Laos, visiting a friend is not usually timed around meals or weekdays. The common expectation is to visit before a meal or on a weekend. Since the person wants to visit a friend who lives nearby, the best time would be before a meal or on a weekend. This fits the local preference for visiting at those times. Visiting before a meal or on a weekday would not match the usual practice there.

In Lebanon, swearing in front of a woman is not the usual expectation. Many men there avoid using profanity when a woman is present. So when the man drops the box and feels pain, he should hold back any curse words. Instead, he can express his discomfort in a more neutral way, perhaps by saying something like "ouch" or "that hurt." This fits the situation because it shows consideration for the female colleague without resorting to language that might be seen as inappropriate.

In Lebanon, the idea that people are expected to be reserved toward strangers does not reflect the usual practice. When a traveler arrives at a family's home in the evening, tired from a long journey, the family is generally expected to be hospitable and welcoming. This means offering the traveler a place to stay, food, and a warm reception rather than keeping a distance. The family should therefore invite the traveler to stay, offer food, and welcome them warmly. Doing so aligns with the common expectation of openness and generosity toward guests in Lebanese homes.

In North Macedonia, a visitor is not expected to arrive without prior notice, as spontaneous visits are not welcome. The common expectation is to arrange the visit in advance, giving the host time to prepare. Therefore, the visitor should contact the friend beforehand to agree on a suitable time. This shows consideration for the host's schedule and avoids causing inconvenience. Simply showing up without prior notice would likely be seen as inconsiderate.

In Malta, an elderly neighbor would not typically greet a young adult using the person's formal given name. The common expectation is that older people use the person's first name when greeting. So in this situation, the elderly neighbor would most likely greet the young adult by their first name. This fits the situation because the neighbor is elderly and the young adult is a neighbor, and the first-name greeting is the usual practice in such interactions.

In Malta, leaving the shoulders uncovered when entering a church is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to cover the shoulders, as a sign of respect for the sacred space. Therefore, the person should cover their shoulders before entering the church. This shows consideration for the local custom and helps maintain a respectful atmosphere during the visit.

In Myanmar, a gift is not usually opened right away when it is handed over. The common expectation is to set the gift aside and open it later, often in private. So the coworker should accept the gift politely, thank the colleague, and then open it later, away from the group. Opening it immediately in front of everyone would go against this preference.

In Nepal, the idea that people generally avoid asking friends for personal favours and support is not accurate. Reliability and loyalty toward close others are important, so friends are expected to help one another when needed. When someone needs help moving to a new apartment and a friend is available, the appropriate action is to ask that friend for help. Declining to ask would go against the expectation of mutual support and could be seen as failing to be dependable. Therefore, the person should ask the friend for help moving to the new apartment.

In Papua New Guinea, people often prefer to communicate indirectly, especially when the topic is general or routine. This means that when a colleague asks for feedback on a routine project update, the team member is likely to respond in a way that hints at the feedback rather than stating it directly. A direct statement of the feedback would feel too blunt or confrontational in this context. Instead, the team member should offer a response that suggests the feedback without explicitly saying it. This approach aligns with the common expectation of indirect communication in Papua New Guinea and helps maintain a comfortable working relationship.

In Palestine, the idea that newlyweds usually move into a home of their own after marriage is not the common expectation. It is more usual for a newlywed couple to live with the bride's family for the first few years. This arrangement is a widely accepted practice, not a strict rule, and it allows the couple to be close to the bride's family during the early years of their marriage. Therefore, in this situation, the couple should live with the bride's family for the first few years. Moving into a home of their own right away would be less typical and might not align with the usual family arrangement.

In Saudi Arabia, tipping is not routine or expected; it is generally not done. The customer should therefore leave without tipping. Leaving a tip would not fit the common practice there and could be seen as unnecessary or even awkward. The appropriate action is simply to thank the staff and depart after paying the bill.

In Somalia, a verbal greeting without physical contact is not the usual way for men to greet each other when they meet for the first time in a business setting. The common expectation is that men shake hands when they first meet. Therefore, in this situation, the two men should shake hands. A verbal greeting alone would not fit the standard practice for a first meeting between men in Somalia.

In Serbia, a colleague's frown during a presentation is not usually a personal slight. People there tend to treat facial expressions as a general reaction to the content rather than a judgment of the person. The presenter should therefore read the frown as a sign that the presentation may not be going well, perhaps because the material is unclear or unconvincing. Taking the frown personally would be a mistake, since it would assume the colleague is upset with the presenter rather than with the presentation itself. The better approach is to see the frown as feedback about the content and adjust the presentation accordingly.

In Thailand, addressing a colleague by only their first name without any title is not the usual practice. People there commonly use a title together with the person's first name, such as 'Khun' followed by the first name. This form of address is a common expectation in professional settings, especially when meeting someone for the first time. Therefore, the employee should address the colleague by using a title together with the first name. Using only the first name without a title would be less appropriate in this context.

In Thailand, directly pointing out a colleague's mistake during a team presentation is not the usual way to handle such a situation. Avoiding causing offense or disruption to another person is important, so a coworker would typically refrain from correcting the mistake in front of others. Instead, the coworker should let the mistake go and not mention it during the presentation. This approach preserves the colleague's dignity and maintains a harmonious atmosphere in the team. After the presentation, if necessary, the coworker might address the mistake privately and discreetly, but not in a way that embarrasses the colleague in front of the group.

In Timor-Leste, the left hand is not the usual choice for passing objects. The common expectation is to use the right hand when giving something to another person. So in this situation, the person should pass the document with their right hand. Using the left hand could be seen as less appropriate or even disrespectful in this context.

In Tonga, when two women meet for the first time at a community gathering, the common greeting is a kiss on the cheek. This practice is a familiar way for newly acquainted women to acknowledge each other in social settings. Therefore, they should greet each other with a kiss on the cheek. A handshake would not be the typical greeting in this context.

In Ukraine, avoiding direct eye contact is not the usual expectation during a conversation. People there generally expect to see the other person's eyes when speaking, as it signals engagement and sincerity. So in this work conversation with a colleague, the person should maintain direct eye contact while speaking. Looking away or avoiding the colleague's gaze could be read as disinterest or lack of confidence. Direct eye contact is the appropriate way to show that the person is paying attention and taking the matter seriously.

In Ukraine, suggesting a meeting is not a free pass to put it off indefinitely. Reliability and loyalty toward others matter, so once you propose a meeting, you are expected to follow through. The person who suggested the meeting should promptly arrange the details, such as time and place, and confirm them with the colleague. Delaying the organization would signal a lack of dependability and could damage the working relationship. Therefore, the appropriate action is to organize the meeting promptly and confirm the details with the colleague.

In Samoa, land is not usually passed down to the eldest child regardless of behavior. The common expectation is that land is passed down to the child who is most deserving, and this is often determined by the child's behavior. Therefore, the parent should allocate the land to the child who is most deserving, based on their conduct. Giving it to the eldest child without regard to their behavior would not align with this practice.

In Samoa, raising one's voice in public is not the usual way to handle strong emotions. Avoiding disruption or offense to others is important, so people are expected to keep their composure even when upset. In a public market, the person should stay calm and not raise their voice, even after being overcharged. Instead, they might quietly address the issue with the vendor or simply walk away. Raising their voice would draw attention and disturb others, which goes against the value of not causing offense.

In Argentina, a gift is not usually set aside to be opened later. The common expectation is that the host opens the present right away, in front of the guest. This allows the giver to see the recipient's reaction and share in the moment. So the host should open the gift immediately upon receiving it. Setting it aside would miss the opportunity for that shared acknowledgment.

In Argentina, the idea that personal space tends to be ample during a conversation is not accurate. People there commonly stand quite close to one another while talking, even in a quiet office setting. For two colleagues discussing a work project, this means they should stand quite close to each other. Keeping a large distance would feel unnecessarily distant and could make the interaction seem cold or unfriendly. Standing close is a normal and expected part of conversation in Argentina.

In Argentina, clearing one's throat at the table is not considered acceptable; it is generally seen as rude. The expectation is to avoid actions that might disturb or offend others during a shared meal. Therefore, the person should refrain from clearing their throat. Instead, they might try to suppress the tickle or excuse themselves briefly if necessary. This approach respects the common preference for quiet and considerate behavior at the dinner table.

In Argentina, the idea that men are expected to wear casual, light-coloured clothing in business settings is not accurate. The common expectation is that men dress formally, wearing dark-coloured suits and ties. For his first day at a new office job, he should therefore wear a dark-coloured suit and tie. This choice aligns with the professional standard in Argentina and shows he takes the workplace seriously. Casual, light-coloured clothing would likely be seen as underdressed and could create a poor first impression.

In Germany, giving a polite but evasive answer to a serious question is not the usual expectation. When a colleague asks for feedback on a project proposal with significant flaws, the person is expected to be direct and honest. The appropriate response is to point out the flaws in the proposal. This approach fits the situation because it addresses the colleague's request for feedback in a straightforward manner, which is valued in German professional communication. Avoiding the flaws would be seen as unhelpful and could undermine the colleague's ability to improve the proposal.

In Germany, the idea that couples usually get married without living together first is not accurate. It is common for couples to live together for a period before deciding to marry. This allows them to experience daily life together and build a solid foundation. For this couple, who have been dating for two years and are discussing their future, the most likely step would be to move in together before getting married. This approach is widely accepted and seen as a practical way to test compatibility and strengthen their relationship. Getting married without cohabitation would be less typical in this context.

In Egypt, when a guest is eating a meal prepared by the host, it is common to express appreciation in a way that feels less direct and more conversational. Rather than stating outright that the food is delicious, the guest is expected to phrase the compliment as a question. For example, the guest might ask, "Is this not delicious?" or "Is this not good?" This form of compliment is seen as more polite and considerate, as it allows the host to share the credit or downplay the praise. Therefore, the guest should compliment the food by asking a question rather than making a direct statement.

In Egypt, the idea that female friends and relatives greet each other with only a handshake is not accurate. It is common for close female friends and relatives to greet each other with a kiss on the cheek. This is a warm and familiar way to show affection and closeness. Therefore, when two female friends meet after a long time apart, they would typically greet each other with a kiss on the cheek. A simple handshake without kissing would feel too formal and distant for such a relationship.

In Ethiopia, drinking coffee quickly is not the usual way to show appreciation. The common expectation is to drink the coffee slowly, savoring each sip. This allows the guest to fully enjoy the coffee and acknowledge the host's hospitality. Therefore, the guest should drink the coffee slowly, taking their time to appreciate the flavor and the moment.

In Indonesia, steady, unbroken eye contact with a peer during a conversation is not the usual expectation. People there tend to avoid looking directly at their peers for long periods, as prolonged eye contact can feel too intense or confrontational in a workplace setting. The listener should therefore look away from time to time, perhaps by glancing down or to the side, to soften the interaction. This behavior fits the situation because it shows awareness of the other person's comfort and helps keep the exchange relaxed and respectful. Maintaining steady eye contact would likely feel too direct and could make the colleague uneasy.

In India, a junior employee is not expected to take a phone call during a team meeting. Avoiding disruption to others is important, so the junior member should let the call go to voicemail. This shows consideration for the group and respects the meeting's flow. Answering the phone would interrupt the discussion and draw attention away from the meeting. Therefore, the junior employee should ignore the call and continue to focus on the meeting.

In India, a wedding is not usually completed in a single day. The customary expectation is that the wedding festivities will extend over several days, often three or more. This allows for multiple ceremonies, rituals, and celebrations that are part of the tradition. For this couple planning their wedding, they would typically arrange the schedule to cover multiple days rather than trying to fit everything into one day. A single-day schedule would not reflect the usual practice and might leave out important parts of the celebration.

In India, the idea that people may stand closer to those of the opposite gender is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to keep a greater distance from someone of the opposite gender. So in this office hallway chat, the man and the woman should maintain a greater distance from each other. Standing closer would not fit the usual preference for personal space between men and women in this setting.

In India, business dealings are often approached with a preference for thoroughness and protection of one's interests. When a business partner proposes a simple agreement, it is common to expect a more comprehensive contract document to ensure clarity and safeguard one's position. Therefore, the person should request a more comprehensive contract document. Accepting only the simple agreement as is would leave room for ambiguity and could expose interests to unnecessary risk. A detailed contract aligns with the expectation of careful preparation and helps prevent misunderstandings in the collaboration.

In Japan, when a man performs a standing bow, it is common for him to stand with his feet together. This posture is a standard expectation for a formal greeting such as a bow. Therefore, he should position his feet together rather than with one foot slightly forward. Standing with feet together aligns with the customary way of bowing in this context.

In Japan, the idea that people stand close to one another where possible is not the usual expectation. Personal space is generally respected, and people tend to keep a comfortable distance from others. In an office building, while waiting for an elevator, two colleagues would typically maintain a moderate distance between each other. Standing too close could feel intrusive or uncomfortable. Therefore, they should keep a moderate distance between each other while waiting.

In Japan, bowing while walking is not the usual practice. People generally walk upright and bow only when stopping or greeting someone. When passing an acquaintance in a hallway, the person should walk past without bowing. Bowing while walking would be awkward and not in line with common expectations. A simple nod or a brief pause to acknowledge the acquaintance is more appropriate in this situation.

In Japan, a standing bow is not typically performed with the feet apart. The common expectation is that a woman stands with her feet together when bowing. This posture is considered appropriate for the gesture and is widely observed in professional and social settings. Therefore, she should position her feet together rather than apart. Standing with feet apart would not align with the usual practice for a standing bow in Japan.

In Japan, the idea that the husband usually assumes the responsibility of managing the family budget is not the common expectation. Instead, it is generally the wife who takes on this role. This arrangement is a widely recognized part of household responsibilities in Japan. Therefore, in this situation, the wife should be responsible for managing the family budget. This fits the usual practice rather than the opposite.

In Japan, after ringing the bell at a shrine, it is not the usual expectation to remain silent. Visitors are generally expected to clap twice and bow before leaving. This practice is a common way to show respect and gratitude at the shrine. Therefore, the visitor should clap twice and bow before departing. Remaining silent would not align with this customary gesture.

In Japan, bowing while seated on a chair is not the usual way to greet someone. The common expectation is to stand up when greeting, as a sign of respect. So the visitor should stand up to bow to the host. This shows proper courtesy in a Japanese setting.

In Japan, refusing a gift from someone who is higher ranking is not generally considered acceptable; it can be seen as a slight to the manager's authority and generosity. Avoiding offense or disruption to another person is important, so the junior employee should accept the gift. Accepting shows respect for the manager's position and maintains a harmonious relationship. Declining the gift, even politely, could be interpreted as rejecting the manager's goodwill. Therefore, the junior employee should accept the gift to avoid causing offense.

In Japan, the idea that women commonly wear bright, colourful clothing in business settings is not accurate. The usual expectation is that women wear dark, neutral colours in business settings. For her first day at a new office job, she should choose dark, neutral clothing such as black, navy, or grey. This fits the common practice in Japanese offices, where understated, dark colours are the standard for professional attire. Bright, colourful clothing would be less typical and might not align with the office's expectations.

In Japan, looking directly into the other person's eyes is not the usual way to show attention during a conversation. People there often avoid prolonged eye contact, as it can feel too intense or confrontational. Instead, the listener is expected to direct their gaze slightly away from the colleague's eyes, perhaps to the side or down. This indirect gaze is a common way to signal respect and attentiveness without staring. So in this situation, the listener should look slightly away from the colleague's eyes rather than directly into them.

In Japan, the idea that little emphasis is placed on bathing oneself is not accurate. Maintaining personal cleanliness is important there, and bathing is treated as a regular and necessary part of daily life. A household would therefore be expected to make time for regular bathing as part of its daily routine. This means not skipping it unless there is a strong reason, and ensuring it is a consistent practice. Treating bathing as optional or unimportant would go against the common expectation in Japan.

In Japan, the idea that people maintain a closer distance from acquaintances is not accurate. The usual expectation is the opposite: people keep a greater distance from acquaintances. Since these two colleagues have worked together for only a few months, they are still in the acquaintance stage rather than close friends. Therefore, they should stand farther apart while talking. Standing too close would feel intrusive and uncomfortable in this situation.

In Russia, the idea that couples generally meet through online dating platforms is not accurate. The common expectation is that people meet their partners through social circles, such as friends, family, or colleagues. For a young single woman looking for a partner, this means she would most likely go about meeting someone through her social network. She might be introduced by friends or family, or she could meet someone through work or shared activities. Relying on online dating platforms would be less typical in this context. Therefore, the most likely approach for her would be to meet someone through her social circles.

In Russia, the idea that men are not expected to help women carry items is not accurate. Supporting the welfare of others is important there, and this often shows up in everyday gestures like helping someone who is struggling. When a woman is carrying a heavy box, a man is generally expected to offer to help. So in this situation, the man should offer to help the woman carry the heavy box. Not offering would go against the common expectation of caring for others in that context.

In Russia, following formal rules and procedures is important, so a manager is expected to present a new procedure as an official requirement rather than a personal suggestion. This approach shows that the procedure is not optional and that everyone is expected to comply. The manager should therefore explain the procedure as a mandatory requirement that must be followed. Presenting it as a personal recommendation would undermine its authority and could be seen as not taking the matter seriously. By framing it as a requirement, the manager aligns with the common expectation of adhering to formal rules and procedures.

In Russia, there is a common belief that speaking too confidently about good fortune can attract bad luck. When someone says that their child has been healthy all year, it is seen as tempting fate. To prevent bad luck, the friend should knock on wood. This small gesture is a way of acknowledging the good fortune while warding off any negative consequences. It is a widely recognized practice in Russia, and many people do it without thinking. Not knocking on wood would leave the friend open to the possibility of inviting bad luck.

In Russia, a small, modest bouquet is not the usual choice when visiting a friend who has just moved into a new apartment. The common expectation is to bring a large bouquet, as this is seen as a generous and thoughtful gesture. A large bouquet shows that the colleague cares and wants to celebrate the friend's new home. Therefore, the colleague should bring a large bouquet to fit this situation.

In Russia, a guest is not left without any refreshments when visiting a home. The common expectation is that the host will offer something to eat or drink, even for a casual visit. So the host should offer the guest refreshments, such as tea, coffee, or a snack. Not offering anything would feel inhospitable and would not match what is usually expected in this setting.

In Russia, the idea that women are expected to have a practical, androgynous look is not accurate. The common expectation is that women dress in a feminine and attractive manner. For a family gathering, she should choose an outfit that is feminine and attractive, such as a dress or a skirt and blouse. This fits the situation because it shows care for her appearance and aligns with what is generally considered appropriate for such occasions in Russia. A practical, androgynous outfit would not match this expectation and might seem out of place.

In Brazil, leaving after the main course is not the usual expectation at a dinner party. The common practice is to stay until the end of the meal, which includes the dessert course. So the guest should remain at the table and wait for dessert to be served. Leaving early would be seen as abrupt and could be taken as a sign that the guest did not enjoy the meal or the company. Staying until the end shows consideration for the host and the other guests.

In Chile, a guest is not expected to decline a drink that is offered. When a host offers a drink, it is generally seen as a gesture of hospitality and welcome, and the guest is expected to accept it. Therefore, the guest should accept the drink. Politely declining could be perceived as rejecting the host's kindness or not appreciating the hospitality. Accepting the drink shows respect for the host's effort and helps maintain a warm and friendly atmosphere.

In Colombia, chewing gum with one's mouth open is not considered acceptable. The common expectation is to keep the mouth closed while chewing. Therefore, the person should chew the gum with their mouth closed. This practice is seen as more polite and considerate in a shared office setting. Chewing with an open mouth could be perceived as rude or distracting to colleagues.

In Fiji, people generally avoid prolonged direct eye contact during conversations. This is a common expectation in everyday interactions, including workplace discussions. When speaking with a colleague about a work matter, the person would most likely maintain eye contact briefly and then look away or down. Holding steady eye contact for an extended period could feel uncomfortable or too intense in this setting. Therefore, the person would probably use intermittent eye contact rather than a fixed gaze.

In the United Kingdom, being completely direct and blunt is not the usual expectation when a colleague presents a flawed proposal. People there generally value avoiding offense and disruption in interpersonal interactions, so a response is expected to be tactful and considerate. The person should therefore point out the flaws in a tactful and considerate manner, perhaps by softening the criticism or framing it as a shared problem to solve. A blunt approach would likely be seen as rude and could damage the working relationship.

In Greece, using formal titles and surnames with an older neighbor is not the usual way to show respect. The common expectation is to use the person's first name, even when they are older and not a relative. So the young adult should address the older neighbor by their first name. This fits the situation because the neighbor is not a relative, and using a formal title would feel distant and overly stiff in a casual shopping encounter.

In Croatia, a guest at a dinner party is not free to choose any seat they like. The usual expectation is that guests wait to be seated by the host. So the guest should wait for the host to indicate where to sit. Choosing a seat on their own would go against this common practice.

In Hungary, the usual way to introduce yourself is to give your surname first, followed by your given name. This is a common expectation in formal and professional settings, such as meeting colleagues for the first time. Therefore, the employee would most likely say their surname first, then their given name. Introducing the given name first would be less typical and might sound unusual in this context.

In Hungary, using a first name right away with a senior colleague is not the usual way to show respect. Avoiding offense or disruption in interpersonal interactions matters, so people tend to be more formal when they first meet someone. The common expectation is to use the person's title and surname until they invite you to use their first name. Therefore, the new employee should address the senior colleague by their title and surname. This approach fits the situation because it shows consideration for the senior colleague's position and avoids presuming familiarity.

In Israel, interruptions during conversation are not rare; they are a common part of everyday interaction. When a colleague is speaking and another has a thought to add, the second colleague is likely to interrupt the first colleague to add the thought. This is not seen as rude but as a natural way to engage in the discussion. The expectation is that the conversation can flow freely, with people jumping in when they have something to say. Therefore, the second colleague would probably interject rather than wait for a pause.

In South Korea, a father is not expected to stand back and let his child handle bullying alone. Protecting the welfare of close family members is important, so a father is expected to be protective of his children. When his child is being bullied, the father should step in and confront the older children. This shows that he cares for his child's safety and well-being. Letting the child handle the problem on their own would go against the expectation of being a protective father.

In Laos, it is not usual to visit someone without making arrangements in advance. People there generally expect a visitor to contact the friend first, often by phone, to arrange the visit. This allows the friend to be ready and to know when to expect the person. So the person should call the friend before going over. Going without calling would likely be seen as inconsiderate, since it does not give the friend a chance to prepare or decline.

In Mexico, the idea that people are expected to proceed in order of arrival regardless of age does not reflect the usual expectation. Avoiding offense or disruption to another person is important, and this is especially true when an elderly person is involved. It is common to expect the younger person to let the elderly person go first. Therefore, the young adult should let the elderly person go through the doorway first. Proceeding through the doorway first would risk causing offense or disruption to the elderly person, which is something people generally try to avoid.

In North Macedonia, close friends and family commonly greet each other with a handshake or a brief hug. This is a warm and familiar way to show affection and pleasure at seeing one another. Since the two people in this situation are close friends meeting after a month apart, a handshake or a brief hug would be appropriate. A kiss on the cheek would be less typical for close friends in this context. Therefore, they should greet each other with a handshake or a brief hug.

In Malta, bowing is not the usual way for professionals to greet each other at a first business meeting. The common expectation is a handshake, which is a standard and accepted form of greeting in professional settings. Therefore, the two professionals would typically shake hands when they meet. This practice reflects the general preference for a direct and straightforward greeting in business contexts.

In Myanmar, a smile is not always a sign of happiness or amusement. It can also be used to mask discomfort or embarrassment, especially in awkward or tense situations. When a colleague spills coffee on a shared document during a meeting, the moment is likely to be embarrassing for them. A smile in this context would probably be interpreted as a way to cover up that discomfort rather than as genuine amusement. Therefore, the colleague's smile would likely be seen as a way to mask discomfort or embarrassment.

In the Netherlands, arriving late without prior notice is not acceptable, even if the delay is short. Avoiding inconvenience or disruption to others is important, so people are expected to let others know if they will be delayed. The colleague should therefore contact the client as soon as possible to explain the delay and give an estimated arrival time. This shows consideration for the client's time and helps maintain a professional relationship. Simply arriving late without any notice would likely be seen as rude and disrespectful.

In the Netherlands, it is not uncommon for couples to display affection in public. On a sunny afternoon in a park, a couple would likely hold hands or kiss while walking together. This kind of physical closeness is generally accepted and seen as a normal part of a relationship. Therefore, the customary behavior for the couple would be to show affection openly, rather than keeping their distance.

In Nepal, pants or skirts are commonly worn above the knee for casual social outings, especially on a warm day. This preference reflects a relaxed and practical approach to clothing in informal settings. For this situation, the person should choose pants or a skirt that go above the knee. A length at or below the knee would be less typical for a casual social outing in Nepal.

In Nepal, using either hand when handing something to a colleague is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to use the right hand or both hands, as the left hand is generally reserved for unclean tasks. Therefore, the person should use the right hand or both hands to hand the document. This shows respect and aligns with local customs. Using the left hand alone would be seen as inappropriate in this context.

In Peru, a handshake is not the usual greeting between women friends. Among women, a common greeting is a kiss on the cheek. So when these two women meet on the street after a long time, they should greet each other with a kiss on the cheek. A handshake would feel too formal and distant for friends in this situation.

In Poland, pointing with a single finger is not the usual way to indicate something; it can come across as rude or accusatory. The common expectation is to use an open hand or a nod of the head instead. So when a colleague asks where the projector screen is, the person should gesture toward it with an open hand or a slight nod. This approach is more polite and aligns with how people generally communicate in Polish meetings. Using a single finger would likely be seen as impolite or confrontational.

In Portugal, keeping a hat on when entering a church is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to remove a hat or headpiece before stepping inside. For a man attending a wedding, this means he should take off his hat as he enters the church. Doing so shows respect for the sacred space and aligns with the local custom. Keeping the hat on would be seen as disregarding that practice.

In Romania, a guest is not expected to light up without first checking with the host. Avoiding offense or disruption to another person matters, so it is common to ask whether smoking is acceptable. The guest should therefore ask the host for permission before smoking. This shows consideration for the host's preferences and the household. Smoking without asking could be seen as presumptuous or disrespectful.

In Singapore, giving a gift with one hand is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to use both hands when handing over a present. This shows care and respect in the exchange. Therefore, the colleague should give the wrapped present using both hands. Using one hand might come across as careless or disrespectful in this setting.

In Somalia, the idea that only the parents are responsible for a child’s parenting and upbringing does not reflect the common expectation. Supporting the welfare of children is important, and this often means that others in the community feel a shared responsibility for a child’s behavior. When a child misbehaves in a public place while the parents are present, it is not unusual for someone other than the parents to step in and correct the child. This correction is seen as a way of caring for the child and maintaining proper conduct in public. Therefore, in this situation, someone other than the parents should correct the child, as this aligns with the community’s shared role in raising children.

In Somalia, it is not uncommon to slip praise of Allah into casual conversation. When two colleagues are chatting during a break about their weekend plans, one colleague might say something like "Mashallah" or "Alhamdulillah" while speaking. This is a natural part of everyday speech and does not disrupt the friendly exchange. Therefore, one colleague would be likely to slip praise of Allah into the conversation.

In Sweden, standing close together, within an arm's length, is not the usual expectation during conversations. People there generally prefer to keep a bit more distance, about an arm's length apart, when chatting. So in a break room between two colleagues, that would be the customary amount of personal space. It allows both people to feel comfortable without intruding on each other's personal bubble.

In Syria, the idea that children are not expected to show particular respect to their elders is not accurate. Avoiding offense or disruption toward others is important, and this is especially true in family settings. Children are expected to show particular respect to their elders, and this expectation is particularly strong at family gatherings. Therefore, the child should show particular respect to the elderly relative. Behaving as if no special respect is needed would risk causing offense and disrupting the family gathering.

In Türkiye, public drunkenness is not generally accepted, and it is especially frowned upon for women. The claim that it is accepted for women misreads the local expectation. Avoiding behavior that could offend or disrupt others is important there, so getting visibly drunk in a crowded festival would likely be seen as inappropriate. The woman should stop drinking before she becomes visibly drunk. Continuing to drink until visibly drunk would risk drawing disapproval and disrupting the social atmosphere.

In Taiwan, the idea that men should primarily care for children does not reflect the usual expectation. Supporting the welfare of close family members is important, and this often means that women are seen as the primary caregivers. There is a general expectation for women to care for children. In this situation, the woman should primarily care for the child. This fits the common preference for the mother to take on the main childcare responsibilities. Having the man primarily care for the child would go against this widely held expectation.

In Venezuela, the idea that the couple is usually expected to pay for their own wedding does not reflect the common expectation. Maintaining inherited family practices is important there, and weddings are traditionally seen as a family affair rather than a couple's sole responsibility. The families of the bride and groom are usually expected to pay for the wedding. Therefore, in this situation, the families of the couple are expected to pay for the wedding, not the couple themselves.

In Samoa, the idea that shoes are usually kept on when entering a dwelling is not the common expectation. The usual practice is to remove shoes before stepping inside. For a visitor arriving at a friend's house for a casual visit, this means taking off their shoes at the door. Keeping shoes on would go against the local custom and could be seen as bringing dirt into the home. Removing shoes shows consideration for the host and the cleanliness of the living space.

In Samoa, the idea that people may choose not to attend church on Sundays is not the usual expectation. Maintaining inherited religious practices is important there, and Sunday is widely treated as a day for communal worship. The family would therefore be expected to attend church on Sunday morning. This fits the situation because the family is deciding how to spend their Sunday morning, and attending church is the customary choice. Choosing not to go would go against the common practice and the value placed on tradition.

In South Africa, the idea that people generally prefer written messages for sensitive updates is not accurate. The common expectation is to communicate through face-to-face conversation when possible. For a sensitive project update, the team member should therefore speak with the colleague in person. This approach fits the situation because it allows for direct exchange and immediate clarification, which is valued in such interactions. Choosing a written message instead would not align with the preference for in-person communication in this context.

In Zimbabwe, greetings are commonly performed in order of social status, with the oldest person being greeted first. This practice reflects a general expectation of showing respect to elders in social interactions. When a group of people of different ages meet for the first time at a community gathering, they should greet the oldest person first, then proceed to the younger individuals. Greeting the youngest first would go against this common expectation and could be seen as disregarding the respect due to older members of the community.

In Zimbabwe, a light handshake with the left hand is not the usual way to greet someone in a professional setting. The common expectation is a firm handshake with the right hand. When a man meets a new colleague for the first time, he should offer a firm handshake using his right hand. This shows confidence and respect, which are important in professional interactions. A light left-handed handshake might be seen as weak or insincere. Therefore, the man should greet the colleague with a firm right-handed handshake.

In Argentina, avoiding personal questions is not the usual expectation when someone has just returned from a trip. It is common and polite to ask about the trip, showing interest in the other person's experience. The colleague should ask the returning colleague about the trip. This fits the situation because the trip is a recent, personal event that the other colleague can naturally inquire about. Not asking could seem distant or uninterested, which is less polite in this context.

In Argentina, the idea that colleagues would keep physical distance and avoid touch while chatting in the office kitchen is not accurate. It is common for people to stand close to one another and to touch each other while communicating. So in this situation, the colleague would most likely stand close to the other person and touch them while talking. This behavior fits the expectation that physical closeness and touch are normal parts of conversation there. Maintaining distance and avoiding touch would feel less typical for this kind of interaction.

In Argentina, the idea that people are expected to rely on their own efforts when seeking opportunities does not reflect the usual practice. Networking and personal connections are important, and people generally expect to be helped by others when looking for a job. The person should ask friends, family, and colleagues for help in finding a job. This approach fits the situation because it aligns with the common expectation of seeking assistance from one's network rather than working alone. Relying solely on one's own efforts would not match the typical way job searches are conducted there.

In Argentina, blowing one's nose at the table is not considered acceptable; it is generally seen as rude. The expectation is to excuse yourself and leave the table before doing so. Therefore, the person should excuse themselves and go to the restroom to clear their nose. This approach respects the shared meal and the comfort of the other diners. Staying at the table and blowing the nose would likely be viewed as impolite.
