Using white, blue, or black would risk sending an unintended message of sadness or bad luck.

In Cyprus, the idea that favours should be granted only on the basis of formal rules and merit does not reflect the usual workplace expectation. Loyalty and preferential support toward close others are important, so a manager is generally expected to show favouritism toward close friends. In this situation, the manager should approve the request for a flexible work schedule if the employee is a close friend. Approving based on merit alone would overlook the value placed on personal relationships and could be seen as failing to support a friend.

In Fiji, the idea that people are not expected to be religious or actively observant is not accurate. Maintaining inherited religious practices is important there, and attending weekly religious services is a common expectation. A young adult moving to a new neighborhood would therefore be expected to attend weekly religious services. This fits the situation because the young adult is considering whether to attend, and the expectation is to participate in these services. Not attending would go against the value placed on continuing religious traditions.

In Fiji, a village's ladies' area is not open to both men and women. The common expectation is that only women are allowed to enter this designated space. Therefore, in this situation, only women are permitted to enter the clearly marked area for women. A man entering such an area would go against the usual practice in Fijian villages.

In France, the idea that weekend visits to parents and grandparents are uncommon is not accurate. Maintaining close family ties and supporting the well-being of older relatives is important there. Because of this, young adults who have moved to a nearby town often make a point of visiting their parents and grandparents on the weekend. The person in this situation would most likely spend the weekend visiting their parents and grandparents. Choosing to spend the weekend with friends instead would go against the common expectation of staying connected with older family members.

In France, the idea that many couples prefer to wait until marriage before living together is not accurate. It is common for couples to live together before getting married. For this couple, who have been dating for two years and are discussing their future living arrangements, a common choice would be to live together before marriage. This arrangement is widely accepted and seen as a natural step in a long-term relationship. Waiting until marriage would be less typical in this context.

In the United Kingdom, asking for help without saying “please” is not acceptable; it is generally seen as rude. Avoiding offense or disruption to others is important, so a request should always include “please.” Therefore, the person should ask the colleague for the pen while saying “please.” This shows consideration for the colleague and fits the common expectation of politeness in British workplaces.

In Greece, addressing a senior colleague by their first name right away is not the usual expectation. People there generally use a person's title and surname when meeting them for the first time, especially if the other person is older or holds a higher position. This practice shows respect and acknowledges the seniority. Therefore, the new employee should address the senior colleague by their title and surname. Using a first name immediately could come across as too familiar or disrespectful in this initial encounter.

In Hungary, adults do not typically greet a teenager by their last name. The common expectation is to use the first name, especially when the teenager is around 15 years old. This reflects a preference for a more personal and informal address in everyday interactions. Therefore, the adult should address the teenager by their first name. Using the last name would feel overly formal and distant in this community event setting.

In Hungary, the idea that one should maintain a standard distance regardless of individual preferences does not reflect the usual expectation. People there generally try to adjust their personal space to what the other person seems comfortable with. So in this first meeting between colleagues, the better approach is to pay attention to the other person's cues and adjust the distance accordingly. Standing at a fixed distance without regard to the other person's comfort would not fit this preference.

In Hungary, a host is not expected to hold back from encouraging a guest to eat more. The common practice is for the host to urge the guest to have another serving, especially after the first plate has been finished. This reflects a warm and generous attitude toward hospitality, where ensuring the guest is well fed is a priority. Therefore, the host should encourage the guest to have another serving. Refraining from urging would go against the usual expectation of a caring host in this setting.

In Ireland, it is not typical to just show up without asking in advance when you want to visit someone. The usual expectation is to contact the person beforehand, often by phone, to arrange the visit. This gives the friend a chance to say whether the time is convenient. So the typical thing to do before visiting is to call the friend in advance to arrange the visit. Showing up without asking would likely be seen as inconsiderate, since it does not respect the friend's schedule or privacy.

In Iran, business meetings are not typically mixed-gender; the common expectation is that men and women participate separately. The team leader should therefore arrange the meeting so that men and women attend in separate rooms. This arrangement reflects a preference for gender segregation in professional settings. Holding a mixed-gender meeting in a single room would not align with this usual practice.

In Iran, burping in front of others is not read as a compliment to the host. It is generally seen as rude, especially at someone's table. The expectation is to avoid burping in front of others, so the person should try to suppress the burp or excuse themselves quietly. This shows consideration for the host and the other guests. Openly burping and treating it as praise would likely be taken as a lack of manners.

In Iran, giving a gift that contains alcohol or pork is not acceptable. These products are considered impure and are avoided in gift-giving. The colleague should therefore choose a gift that does not contain alcohol or pork. This shows consideration for the coworker's religious and cultural sensitivities. A gift with such ingredients would be inappropriate and could cause offense.

In Israel, lavish gifts are not the usual expectation in business contexts. The common practice is to give modest gifts, such as a small box of chocolates or a pen, when meeting a business partner for the first time. A manager should therefore choose a small, thoughtful gift rather than something extravagant. This approach fits the situation because it shows consideration without overstepping professional boundaries. A lavish gift could be seen as excessive or even inappropriate in this setting.

In Israel, scheduling meetings during September and October without regard to Jewish holidays is not acceptable. The High Holy Days, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, fall in this period, and many people observe them. It is expected to avoid scheduling meetings during these holidays. Therefore, the manager should schedule the meetings outside of September and October, or at least check the dates of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur and avoid those days. This shows consideration for the religious observances of team members and is the appropriate approach in Israel.

In Lebanon, declining a favour simply because it is inconvenient is not the usual expectation. When someone asks for help, it is generally seen as a request that should be honoured, even if it requires some effort. The coworker should therefore agree to help move the boxes to the storage room. Politely declining would likely be perceived as unhelpful or rude, since the request is a direct appeal for assistance. Helping is the appropriate response in this situation.

In Sri Lanka, a sensitive project update is not something a manager would typically prefer to handle through email or messaging. The common expectation is to discuss such matters in person, as this allows for a more nuanced and respectful exchange. Therefore, the manager would prefer to conduct the discussion in person. This approach fits the situation because it shows consideration for the colleague and the delicate nature of the update, which is better conveyed through direct interaction.

In Sri Lanka, black and white are not the usual choices for festive occasions like weddings. The common expectation is to avoid these colors for such celebrations. For a wedding celebration, she should choose a color other than black or white. This fits the situation because the outfit is for a festive event, and avoiding black and white aligns with the local preference.

In Myanmar, giving an honest answer that the other person does not want to hear is not the usual expectation. People there generally try to avoid causing offense or disruption, so they often prefer to soften criticism or give a more positive response. In this situation, the coworker should give a positive response, even if the draft proposal has flaws. A blunt, honest assessment could embarrass the colleague and damage the working relationship. A gentle, encouraging reply fits the common preference for maintaining smooth interactions.

In Mauritius, leaving a small shop without any verbal exchange is not the usual expectation. It is common to say 'bonza' when leaving, especially with service providers. This small phrase is a friendly way to acknowledge the service and the interaction. Therefore, the customer is expected to say 'bonza' when leaving. Simply leaving without saying anything would feel abrupt and less polite in this setting.

In Mauritius, close friends of similar age commonly address each other by their first names. This reflects a relaxed and informal style of interaction among peers. In a café setting, one friend would therefore call the other by their first name rather than a more formal title. Using a title would feel distant or overly formal for such a close relationship. The first name is the natural and expected way to speak to a close friend in this situation.

In Malaysia, the left hand is not perfectly acceptable to use alone when giving or receiving objects. The common expectation is to avoid using the left hand alone for such exchanges. Therefore, the colleague should use the right hand to give the document. Using the left hand alone would not align with this preference.

In Malaysia, accepting a gift immediately without any hesitation is not the usual polite way to receive it. The common expectation is to politely decline the gift once or twice before accepting it. This shows humility and avoids appearing overly eager or greedy. So, when the colleague offers the small gift, the coworker should first say something like, "Oh, you shouldn't have," and then accept it after the colleague insists. Accepting right away might come across as too forward or lacking in modesty.

In Malaysia, a new employee is not expected to be very casual and informal in a first meeting with colleagues from another department. The common expectation is to be very formal and polite. This means the employee should use formal language, show respect in their manner, and avoid overly familiar behavior. Being casual and informal could be seen as disrespectful or unprofessional in this setting. Therefore, the employee should behave very formally and politely during the meeting.

In Nepal, direct communication is not the usual expectation in professional relationships, especially when trust is not yet strong or the situation is sensitive. A manager giving feedback about a recent project should therefore avoid blunt or confrontational language. Instead, the manager should communicate the feedback indirectly, perhaps by framing it as a shared concern or by softening the message. This approach respects the relational nature of professional interactions in Nepal and helps maintain harmony. Directness in this context could be seen as too harsh or disrespectful, undermining the working relationship.

In New Zealand, being modest and downplaying achievements is not the usual expectation in a job interview. The common practice is to be self-assured and confident, highlighting one's achievements, qualifications, and ambitions. Therefore, the candidate should confidently present their accomplishments and future goals. This approach fits the situation because it shows the interviewer that the candidate is capable and motivated, which are valued qualities in a professional setting. Downplaying strengths could be seen as lacking confidence or not taking the opportunity seriously.

In Pakistan, beckoning with the palm facing upward and using a single finger is not the usual way to get someone's attention. The common expectation is to use the palm facing downward and to wave the whole hand or use the thumb and index finger together. So, to beckon the colleague across the room, the person should use the palm facing downward and wave the whole hand or use the thumb and index finger together. This approach fits the situation because it is the standard way to call someone over in Pakistan, and it avoids the gesture that is generally considered inappropriate there.

In Peru, using a first name with a lawyer is not the usual way to show respect. The common expectation is to address people by their professional title, such as 'doctor' for a lawyer, unless they invite you to use their first name. So the employee should call the lawyer 'doctor' when speaking to them for the first time. This shows proper respect for the lawyer's profession and is the safer choice in a first meeting.

In the Philippines, a pregnant woman is not generally expected to wear a necklace. The common expectation is that she should avoid wearing one. So for this family gathering, she would typically leave the necklace off. Wearing a necklace would go against the usual practice in this situation.

In the Philippines, it is not the usual practice to open a gift in front of the giver right away. The common expectation is to thank the giver and set the gift aside without unwrapping it. This allows the giver to feel appreciated without the recipient's attention focused on the contents. In this office gathering, the coworker should therefore express thanks and place the wrapped present aside. Opening it immediately would go against the customary courtesy in this setting.

In Papua New Guinea, it is not the case that gifts are commonly given on ordinary visits. The usual expectation is that gifts are reserved for special occasions, such as a birthday or a wedding. For a casual dinner at a friend's home, which is an ordinary visit, bringing a gift would not fit the common practice. The colleague should therefore not bring a gift, as it is not typically expected in this situation.

In Poland, pointing directly at someone's forehead is not a neutral gesture; it is commonly understood as an insult. The gesture is seen as aggressive and disrespectful, especially in a conversation where it singles out the other person. Therefore, in this situation, the gesture would be interpreted as an insult rather than as a neutral or harmless action.

In Portugal, using a first name with a department head on a first meeting is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to address someone by their title and surname, especially in professional settings. This shows respect for the person's position and maintains a formal tone appropriate for a new employee meeting a superior. Therefore, the employee should address the department head by their title and surname. Using a first name right away could be seen as overly familiar or disrespectful in this context.

In Portugal, maintaining one's reputation and dignity is considerably important, so being publicly undermined can feel like a serious slight. When a colleague takes credit for your idea in a team meeting, the expectation is to address the situation promptly and directly rather than letting it go. The person should speak up during the meeting to correct the record and claim the idea as their own. Waiting until after the meeting to do so would risk appearing passive or as if the slight was not worth addressing. By intervening at once, the person defends their standing and ensures they are seen as someone who values their own integrity.

In Palestine, a resident is not expected to give their opinion in short, concise ways during a community meeting. The common preference is to express one's view in a long, detailed manner. Therefore, the resident should speak at length, providing a thorough explanation of their opinion on the proposed local project. This approach aligns with the local expectation of offering a full and elaborated perspective rather than a brief statement.

In Romania, removing a suit jacket during a business meeting is not the usual expectation, even when the wearer feels warm. The common practice is to keep the jacket on unless it is absolutely necessary to take it off, such as for a medical reason. Since the employee is wearing a suit in a business setting, the appropriate choice is to remain in the jacket. Taking it off simply because of warmth would be seen as too casual for the occasion. Therefore, the employee should keep the jacket on and manage the warmth in another way, if possible.

In Romania, the idea that family members should be financially independent and not rely on each other is not the usual expectation. Supporting the well-being of close family members is important, and this often means being willing to help a sibling in need. When a sibling faces a financial difficulty, the young adult is generally expected to offer assistance rather than keep their own finances separate. Helping the sibling is the appropriate response because it shows care and maintains close family bonds. Declining to help would go against the common expectation of mutual support within the family.

In Saudi Arabia, pointing your feet towards other people while sitting is not acceptable. The feet are considered the lowest and least respectful part of the body, so directing them at someone is seen as rude. The common expectation is to keep your feet tucked back or to the side, away from others. Therefore, the person should adjust their position so that their feet are not pointed at anyone in the room. This shows consideration for the people present and avoids causing offense.

In Sudan, remaining seated when greeting an older colleague is not the usual expectation. Avoiding offense or disruption toward others is important, so standing up is a way to show respect. The young employee should therefore stand up when the older colleague enters the room. This gesture acknowledges the older person's presence and avoids the impression of being too casual or disrespectful. Staying seated could be seen as a lack of regard for the older colleague's age and position.

In Sudan, the idea that two friends typically maintain a noticeable distance when sitting is not accurate. Close friends often sit very close to one another, sometimes with their bodies touching. This closeness is a common and accepted way for friends to show comfort and familiarity. In this situation, the two friends would likely sit very close to each other, perhaps with their bodies touching. Sitting at a noticeable distance would feel less natural and might suggest a lack of closeness.

In Singapore, receiving a business card with either hand casually is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to receive the card with both hands or with the right hand only. This shows respect for the giver and the card itself. Therefore, the visitor should accept the card using both hands or the right hand only, rather than using either hand casually.

In Somalia, the idea that cooking and food preparation is a shared responsibility between men and women does not reflect the usual household arrangement. Maintaining inherited family roles is important there, and this includes the traditional division of duties in the kitchen. Women are generally expected to be responsible for cooking and food preparation. For this large family gathering, the women should be responsible for cooking the food. This fits the common expectation that the women handle the meal, while men are not typically involved in this task.

In Somalia, the idea that men and women usually eat together at home is not the common expectation. When a family gathers for a meal with both male and female adult relatives present, it is usual for the men and women to eat in separate rooms. This practice reflects a customary separation of dining spaces rather than a strict rule that every household follows. For this dinner, the seating should therefore be arranged with the men in one room and the women in another. Having everyone share the same room would go against the usual practice in this setting.

In Serbia, the idea that young couples prefer to stay at home and avoid social activities is not accurate. On the contrary, young couples there commonly enjoy going out together, and a Saturday afternoon is a typical time for that. They would most likely go to a cafe or restaurant, as these are popular social settings. Staying at home and avoiding such outings would be less usual for a young couple in Serbia.

In Syria, putting a received business card away immediately is not the usual expectation. The visitor should keep the business card out and examine it carefully. This shows respect for the person who gave it and acknowledges the information on the card. Keeping it out also allows the local counterpart to see that the card is being treated with attention. Therefore, the visitor should not put the card away right away.

In Timor-Leste, being blunt and confrontational in a discussion is not the usual expectation. People there generally value avoiding offense or disruption in their interactions with others. This means that when neighbors disagree about a festival, they should keep the discussion respectful and considerate. They should listen to each other's viewpoints and express their own in a calm, non-confrontational way. A blunt or confrontational approach would likely be seen as disrespectful and could damage the relationship between the neighbors. Therefore, the neighbors should conduct their discussion in a respectful and considerate manner.

In Türkiye, a bow is not the customary greeting when people meet for the first time. The usual practice is to shake hands. So when two colleagues are introduced at a business meeting, they should greet each other by shaking hands. This is the common expectation in such a setting. A bow would not be the typical way to greet someone in this situation.

In Taiwan, placing chopsticks pointing down into an empty bowl is not acceptable. It is commonly seen as a bad omen, as it resembles the way chopsticks are used during funeral rites. The expectation is to avoid this gesture, especially after finishing a meal. Therefore, the person should not place the chopsticks pointing down into the bowl. Instead, they should place them elsewhere, such as on a chopstick rest or on the table, to show respect and avoid any negative association.

In Ukraine, a new business associate is not expected to treat a potential partner with informality from the very first meeting. The common expectation is to begin with formality, using the person's title and surname, until the other party suggests otherwise. This shows respect and maintains a professional distance appropriate for initial business encounters. Therefore, the associate should address the potential partner by their title and surname. Switching to a first name basis too early could be seen as presumptuous or disrespectful.

In Venezuela, the idea that men and women are generally expected to share homemaking responsibilities equally does not reflect the common expectation. Maintaining inherited family roles is important there, and this often means that women are generally expected to take primary responsibility for managing the home. In this situation, with a married couple and young children, the wife would typically be the one to handle the household's day-to-day organization and care. This arrangement is seen as consistent with traditional family roles, where the home is primarily the woman's domain. Therefore, the wife should take primary responsibility for managing the home, as this aligns with the value placed on preserving traditional family roles in Venezuela.

In Venezuela, the idea that adult children are not expected to care for their older family members into their old age is not accurate. Supporting the well-being of close family members is important there, and this often means taking responsibility for an elderly parent who can no longer live alone. The common expectation is that adult children will care for their older family members into their old age. Therefore, the woman should arrange to care for her mother herself, either by having her live with her or by providing daily assistance. This fits the situation because her mother needs daily help and cannot live alone, so the daughter is the one who should step in. Not arranging care would go against the expectation of caring for family members in their old age.

In Samoa, dressing casually when unsure of the appropriate attire is not the usual expectation for a business meeting. The common practice is to dress formally if the person is not sure what to wear. This preference reflects a general tendency toward formality in professional settings. Therefore, the person should choose formal attire for the meeting. Doing so aligns with the local expectation and helps avoid appearing unprepared or disrespectful.

In Argentina, arriving exactly at the stated time for a dinner party is not the usual expectation. Guests are generally expected to arrive about half an hour after the stated time. For a party that starts at 8 PM, a guest should plan to arrive around 8:30 PM. This allows the host extra time to finish preparations without feeling rushed. Arriving at 8:00 PM sharp might catch the host still getting things ready and could be seen as slightly awkward.

In Argentina, arriving late to a business meeting is not generally seen as acceptable. Punctuality is expected in professional settings, and being on time shows respect for the other person's schedule. The associate's arrival at 10:00 AM would be evaluated as punctual, because it meets the expected standard for business engagements. Arriving after 10:00 AM would likely be viewed as disrespectful or careless, as it disregards the agreed-upon time. Therefore, the associate should aim to be on time to make a good impression.

In Argentina, when two friends who are not very close meet at a social gathering, a simple handshake is the common and expected greeting. This reflects a preference for a reserved and formal manner in less intimate relationships. A hug and a kiss on the cheek would be too familiar for friends who are not close. Therefore, they greet each other with a handshake.

In Argentina, a simple handshake without an embrace is not the usual way close friends greet each other. The common expectation among friends and family is to hug and kiss each other on the cheek. So when two close friends meet on the street after a week apart, they should hug and kiss each other on the cheek. This fits the situation because they are close friends, and the greeting reflects the warmth and closeness of their relationship. A handshake without an embrace would feel too formal and distant for such a friendship.

In Germany, introducing humour to lighten a stern conversation is not the usual expectation. People there generally prefer to keep serious discussions focused and without jokes, as humour can be seen as inappropriate or disrespectful in such moments. The team member should therefore refrain from making a joke during the discussion about project delays. Instead, it is better to maintain a serious tone and address the issue directly. This approach aligns with the common preference for seriousness in professional settings in Germany.

In Germany, it is not the usual practice to give flowers still wrapped. The common expectation is to unwrap the bouquet before presenting it. This shows care and allows the recipient to see the flowers properly. Therefore, the guest should unwrap the bouquet before giving it to the host. Giving them wrapped would be seen as less thoughtful in this context.

In Germany, a colleague asking about the realism of a project timeline is not looking for an indirect or modest answer. The expectation is to be straightforwardly honest, so the team member should state directly whether they think the timeline is realistic. Giving an indirect answer would likely be seen as evasive or unhelpful, because clarity and directness are valued in professional communication there. The team member should therefore give a straightforward answer about whether they think the timeline is realistic.

In Germany, using a first name in a formal business setting is not the usual expectation. When meeting a senior manager for the first time, the employee should address the manager by their last name with a title, such as Herr or Frau. This shows respect for the manager's position and maintains a professional distance appropriate to the situation. Addressing the manager by their first name would be too informal and could be seen as presumptuous or disrespectful. Therefore, the employee should use the manager's last name with a title until the manager indicates otherwise.

In Germany, steady eye contact throughout a conversation is not the usual way to show engagement and respect. People there generally prefer to avoid staring, so the person should break eye contact from time to time. This gives the other person space and signals that the interaction is not confrontational. Maintaining steady eye contact could come across as too intense or aggressive. Therefore, the person should break eye contact from time to time during the conversation.

In Egypt, high-pressure tactics are not acceptable in negotiations. The sales representative should avoid pressuring the client to decide. Instead, the representative should present the contract's terms clearly and allow the client time to consider them. This approach respects the client's autonomy and is more likely to build a positive business relationship. Pressuring the client would be seen as disrespectful and could damage the negotiation.

In Egypt, when two women meet for the first time at a community gathering, a warm embrace and a kiss on each cheek is a common and friendly way to greet each other. This physical greeting is a natural expression of warmth and friendliness in such social settings. Therefore, they should greet each other with a warm embrace and a kiss on each cheek. A simple handshake and verbal greeting would feel too formal and distant for this context.

In Egypt, the idea that either hand is acceptable for taking food from a central platter is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to use the right hand for eating communal food. This preference is widely observed during shared meals. Therefore, the person should use their right hand to take food from the platter. Using the left hand would not align with this customary practice.

In Ethiopia, maintaining inherited cultural practices is important, and this is reflected in how elders interact with children. When a young child greets an elderly relative with a bow, it is common for the elderly relative to respond by giving the child a pat on the head. This gesture is a traditional way of acknowledging the child's respectful greeting and showing affection. A verbal response such as saying "hello" would be less typical in this context, as the physical gesture carries the customary meaning. Therefore, the elderly relative would typically pat the child on the head in return.

In Ethiopia, a polite refusal of an offer is not usually taken as a final answer. The host is expected to offer again, and often several times, to show genuine hospitality. So when a guest declines coffee, the host should not simply accept the refusal. Instead, the host should offer the coffee again, perhaps with a warm smile and a repeated invitation. This repeated offering is a common way of expressing care and making the guest feel welcome. Accepting the first refusal and not pressing further could seem as if the host did not really want to serve the guest.

In Ethiopia, it is not the usual practice for an elderly person to shake hands with a young child. Instead, the neighbor would most likely pat the child on the head. This gesture is a common way for elders to show warmth and affection toward children. So when greeting the child, the neighbor would pat the child on the head rather than shake their hand.

In Ethiopia, a direct verbal thank-you is not the usual way to express gratitude for a favor like carrying groceries. The common expectation is to give thanks through a gift, such as food or a small item. So the family should offer the neighbor a gift of food or a small item in return for the help. This fits the situation because the neighbor has done a kind act, and a gift is the appropriate way to acknowledge it. Simply saying thank you would not match the customary practice in Ethiopia.

In Ethiopia, a trilling sound with the tongue is commonly understood as a sign of annoyance or displeasure. When a friend makes this sound, it is not meant as a playful or affectionate gesture. The trilling is a nonverbal way of expressing irritation or dissatisfaction. Therefore, the friend's trilling would most likely be interpreted as a sign of annoyance or displeasure.

In Ethiopia, a new employee is not expected to use a senior colleague's first name right away. The usual practice is to wait for an invitation to be casual, and until then, the new employee should address the senior colleague by their title and surname. This shows respect for the senior colleague's position and maintains a formal tone appropriate for a first meeting. Using a first name immediately, even without an invitation, would be seen as presumptuous and could be considered disrespectful. Therefore, the new employee should use the senior colleague's title and surname until the senior colleague invites them to use their first name.

In Ethiopia, a slight bow without physical contact is not the usual way a young adult greets an elderly neighbor. The common expectation is to greet the elderly with a verbal greeting and a kiss on the forehead. This practice shows respect and affection toward older people. Therefore, the young adult might greet the elderly neighbor with a verbal greeting and a kiss on the forehead. A slight bow without physical contact would not fit this expectation.

In Ethiopia, eating in front of a guest without offering any food is not considered acceptable. Avoiding offense or disruption to others is important, so a host is expected to share what they are eating. The person should offer the guest some of the snack. This shows consideration for the guest and maintains a comfortable interaction. Eating without offering would likely be seen as rude or inconsiderate.

In Indonesia, placing one’s feet on top of the table is not acceptable. The common expectation is to keep your feet on the floor. Therefore, the person should keep their feet on the floor. This shows respect for the meeting room and the people present. Putting feet on the table would be seen as disrespectful and inappropriate.

In Indonesia, a younger employee is not expected to call a senior colleague by their first name. Avoiding offense or disrespect toward others is important, so using a first name with someone older can come across as too familiar or disrespectful. The common expectation is to address an older person by their title and surname, which shows proper respect. Therefore, the young employee should call the senior colleague by their title and surname. This approach fits the situation because it acknowledges the senior colleague's age and position without causing offense.

In Indonesia, a direct approach to corrective remarks is not the usual expectation. People there often prefer to soften criticism so that the other person does not feel embarrassed or lose face. In this situation, the colleague should be told about the mistake in a way that preserves their dignity, perhaps by framing it gently or privately. A blunt correction could be seen as harsh and might damage the working relationship. Therefore, the colleague should be told about the mistake in a way that preserves their dignity.

In Indonesia, it is common for people to arrive late to meetings. This is a widely accepted practice in many professional settings. Therefore, the member should plan to arrive late to the meeting. Arriving on time would be less typical and might not align with the usual expectations in this context.

In Indonesia, the idea that children are not expected to give up their leisure time to raise siblings does not reflect the usual expectation. Supporting the well-being of close family members is important, and this often means older children are expected to help care for younger siblings. When parents ask a teenager to look after their younger siblings on a weekend afternoon, the teenager should agree to do so. Declining to help would go against the common expectation of caring for family members, even when it means giving up personal time. Therefore, the teenager should look after their younger siblings.

In India, a workplace is not typically seen as egalitarian in the sense that open communication is free of age or position-based hierarchy. Respecting hierarchical authority and avoiding offense to those in higher positions are important. Therefore, a junior employee is expected to be careful about how they address a senior colleague, especially in a team meeting. The junior employee should raise the concern privately with the senior colleague after the meeting. This approach shows respect for the senior colleague's position and avoids causing embarrassment in front of others. Pointing out the flaw directly during the meeting could be seen as challenging the senior colleague's authority and disrupting the group's harmony.

In India, the idea that people tend to prioritize their own career advancement over their family's reputation does not reflect the usual expectation. Protecting the family's reputation and public image is important, and this often takes precedence over personal ambitions. A young professional offered a lucrative job that the family considers disreputable would be expected to decline the offer. Accepting the job would risk bringing shame to the family, which is a serious concern. Therefore, the professional should turn down the job to preserve the family's standing.

In India, it is not the usual practice to address a manager by their first name right from the start of a professional relationship. The common expectation is to use the manager's title and surname, such as 'Mr. Sharma' or 'Ms. Patel', until the manager indicates that a first-name basis is acceptable. This shows respect for the hierarchical structure and the manager's position. Therefore, the new employee should address the manager by their title and surname. Using a first name immediately could be seen as overly familiar or disrespectful in this context.

In India, speaking directly to address an error is not the usual way to handle such matters. Avoiding offense and maintaining smooth interpersonal relations is important, so people tend to be indirect and tactful. A team member would therefore not point out the error in front of the colleague or in a blunt manner. Instead, the error should be addressed indirectly and tactfully, perhaps by mentioning it privately or in a way that does not embarrass the colleague. This approach fits the expectation of preserving harmony and avoiding direct confrontation.

In India, receiving a business card with the left hand alone is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to use the right hand or both hands when accepting a card. This shows respect for the person offering the card. Therefore, you should receive the card with your right hand or with both hands. Using only the left hand could be seen as disrespectful in this context.

In Japan, a person with a cold is not expected to go without a face mask in a crowded train. Avoiding harm or discomfort to others is important there, so wearing a mask is the considerate choice. The common expectation is to cover your mouth and nose when you are ill, especially in close quarters like a train. Therefore, the person should put on a face mask before entering the crowded train. Not wearing one would risk spreading germs and would be seen as inconsiderate to fellow passengers.

In Japan, the idea that people at a home altar tend to pray for their own personal success is not the usual expectation. Maintaining inherited religious practices is important there, and this often means praying for the well-being of the family. At a home altar, the person performing the ritual is most likely to pray for the family's well-being. This fits the situation because the family is gathered together, and the ritual is a shared act of care and tradition. Praying for one's own personal success would not align with the common practice of honoring family ties and continuing ancestral customs.

In Japan, pointing one's feet towards someone is not acceptable; it is considered rude. The expectation is to avoid directing the soles of your feet at another person, as this is seen as disrespectful. Therefore, the person should adjust their position so that the soles of their feet are not pointing at the colleague. This could mean sitting cross-legged, tucking the feet to the side, or otherwise angling the feet away. Leaving the feet stretched out with the soles facing the colleague would be inappropriate in this setting.

In Japan, using one's feet to move something is not acceptable. The expectation is to avoid actions that could be seen as disrespectful or offensive. Therefore, the person should pick up the cushion with their hands. Using a foot would be considered inappropriate in this situation.

In Japan, keeping a coat on when entering a building is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to remove the coat before going inside. This applies to office buildings as well as other indoor spaces. Therefore, the visitor should take off the coat before entering the building. Doing so aligns with the local custom and shows consideration for the indoor environment.

In Japan, it is not the case that a person should wait for the counterpart to ask about a delay. Avoiding inconvenience or disruption to others is important, so a person who expects a delay is expected to mention it as soon as possible. The person preparing the report should therefore inform the colleague promptly that the report will be late. Waiting until the colleague asks would leave the colleague waiting unnecessarily and could cause disruption. By informing the colleague early, the person shows consideration for the colleague's time and plans.

In Japan, nodding during a conversation is not primarily a sign of agreement. It is commonly used to show that the listener is paying attention and following the speaker's points. In a business meeting, when a colleague presents a proposal and another colleague nods occasionally, the nodding is most likely interpreted as a sign of active listening and engagement. It does not necessarily mean the listener agrees with the proposal. Therefore, the nodding is most likely interpreted as a sign of active listening and engagement, not agreement.

In Japan, exaggerating or boasting about a gift is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to present the gift modestly, without drawing attention to its value or quality. The colleague should therefore present the gift in a humble way, perhaps with a simple acknowledgment rather than highlighting its features. This approach fits the situation because it shows consideration for the coworker and avoids making the exchange feel self-promotional. A boastful presentation would likely be seen as inappropriate or even offensive in this context.

In Russia, open complaint or anger in public is not common; it is generally avoided. People there tend to keep their frustration to themselves rather than confront the store staff in front of other shoppers. The customer is therefore most likely to leave the store without saying anything about the defective product. This approach fits the expectation of not drawing attention to a problem in a public setting. Confronting the staff openly would go against the preference for maintaining composure and avoiding public displays of dissatisfaction.

In Russia, wearing sporting footwear to a restaurant is not a free pass to enter. Many establishments there have a dress code that includes a ban on athletic shoes, and a person in such footwear is likely to be turned away at the door. The expectation is that a restaurant or bar will not allow entry if the person is wearing sporting footwear. Therefore, the person in this situation is likely to be denied entry.

In Russia, a large bonus is not something people usually highlight in front of colleagues. The common expectation is to avoid drawing attention to one's good fortune, because showing off wealth or well-being is generally seen as inappropriate. So the person should downplay the bonus rather than emphasize it. This fits the situation because openly discussing the amount or bragging about it would go against that preference for modesty. A more fitting approach is to mention the bonus in a low-key way, perhaps without specifying the exact amount, or to steer the conversation to other topics.

In Afghanistan, complimenting something more than once is not the usual way to show appreciation; it can come across as insincere or as if the guest is trying to take the item. The common expectation is to compliment something only once, and then let the matter rest. So after admiring the vase and the host has acknowledged the compliment, the guest should not repeat the compliment. Instead, the guest should move on to another topic or simply continue the conversation without mentioning the vase again. This approach fits the situation because it respects the local preference for a single, sincere compliment rather than repeated praise.

In Austria, omitting a counterpart's title in written correspondence is not the usual practice. The common expectation is to include the title of the person you are addressing, especially when you have not met them before. Therefore, the employee should address the business partner by their title in the email. This shows respect and professionalism, which is important in business communication there. Using the title helps establish a proper tone for the first contact.

In Austria, using the informal 'du' with a new colleague is not the usual way to show respect. Avoiding offense or disruption in interpersonal interactions matters, so people tend to be more formal when they first meet someone. The common expectation is to use the formal 'Sie' until the senior colleague invites you to switch to the informal 'du'. Therefore, the new employee should address the senior colleague using the formal 'Sie'. This approach fits the situation because it shows consideration for the relationship and avoids presuming familiarity.

In Bangladesh, a casual, informal attitude is not the usual expectation when speaking with an elder. Avoiding offense or disruption toward another person is important, so a young employee should show respect to a senior colleague who is much older. The common practice is to use a respectful form of address, such as adding a title or honorific, rather than a first name. Therefore, the young employee should address the senior colleague with a respectful form of address. Using a first name would risk seeming disrespectful and could disrupt the relationship.

In Brazil, gifts are not typically expected in the first few business meetings. The common expectation is that a gift is more appropriate after a relationship has been established, often after several meetings. Since this is only the third meeting, the sales representative should not bring a gift. Doing so could be seen as premature or even inappropriate, as it may imply an attempt to influence the client before a genuine partnership has been built. It is better to focus on building rapport and trust through the discussion itself.

In Canada, it is not the case that people usually do not exchange business cards at meetings. On the contrary, it is common for professionals to exchange business cards when they first meet in a business setting. This practice helps establish contact information and shows a willingness to continue the professional relationship. Therefore, in this situation, the two professionals would typically exchange business cards after introducing themselves. Not doing so might seem less professional or less interested in networking.

In Spain, the idea that friends give gifts to the birthday celebrant is not the usual way to mark the occasion. The common expectation is that the person celebrating their birthday treats their friends to drinks. So in this bar setting, the birthday celebrant would likely buy rounds of drinks for the group. Receiving gifts from friends would be less typical and not the customary gesture. Therefore, the birthday celebrant might mark the occasion by buying drinks for their friends.

In Fiji, a visitor in a village is not expected to shout, run, or be rowdy. The common expectation is to keep calm and quiet while moving through the village. This means walking at a moderate pace and speaking softly, without drawing attention to oneself. Being loud or disruptive would be seen as disrespectful to the community and its daily activities. Therefore, the visitor should behave calmly and quietly while in the village.

In the United Kingdom, spitting on the ground in public is not seen as acceptable; it is generally regarded as disgusting. People there tend to value avoiding actions that might offend or disgust others, so this behavior is likely to draw disapproval. The person's public spitting would probably be viewed as unpleasant and disrespectful to those around them. It would not be considered a normal or acceptable part of street life.

In Greece, keeping feelings to oneself and avoiding direct confrontation is not the usual expectation when a conflict of interest arises. Instead, people are generally expected to be open about their feelings and to confront the issue head-on. In this situation, one partner should openly express their feelings about the competing interests and confront the other partner directly. This approach is seen as more appropriate than bottling up emotions or avoiding the topic. By being open and direct, the partner can address the conflict in a way that is consistent with common expectations in Greece.

In Hong Kong, the number 4 is not considered lucky; it is widely regarded as unlucky. Many people there avoid using the number 4 in addresses, phone numbers, and other significant identifiers. For a family choosing an apartment, this preference would lead them to avoid a floor number containing 4. Therefore, the family would prefer to live on a floor number that does not include the digit 4. Choosing a floor with 4 would go against this common expectation and might be seen as undesirable.

In Hong Kong, sitting with crossed legs in a formal meeting is not generally seen as acceptable and not offensive. It can be perceived as rude or disrespectful, especially in a formal setting with local colleagues. The visitor should therefore avoid sitting with crossed legs and instead keep both feet on the floor. This shows awareness of local expectations and helps maintain a respectful atmosphere in the meeting.

In Hong Kong, a businessperson is not expected to get straight to business without social conversation. It is common to begin with some social talk before moving on to business matters. This helps establish a comfortable atmosphere and shows respect for the relationship. Therefore, the businessperson should engage in some social conversation before discussing business. Skipping this step and immediately discussing business would likely feel abrupt and less appropriate in this setting.

In Hong Kong, the idea that an individual's interests usually come before the group's is not the usual expectation. Loyalty and commitment to the group are important, so people generally try to put the team's needs first when a conflict arises. In this situation, the team member should attend the important team meeting and reschedule the personal appointment. Missing the meeting to keep the personal appointment would go against the common expectation of prioritizing the group's interests.

In Hong Kong, the idea that filial piety focuses only on living family members is not the traditional view. Maintaining inherited cultural practices is important there, and this includes honoring one's ancestors. The traditional expectation is to show respect to deceased family members, especially grandparents, through rituals and remembrance. At a family gathering, the person should therefore perform a ritual to honor their deceased grandparents. This fits the situation because it acknowledges the grandparents' place in the family and keeps the tradition alive. Focusing only on living family members would overlook the duty to the ancestors that is central to filial piety in Hong Kong.

In Croatia, saying grace before a meal is not something the host should do regardless of whether everyone would like to join in the prayer. The common expectation is to ask the guests whether they would like to say grace together. This shows consideration for the guests' preferences and respects their autonomy in religious practice. Therefore, the host should ask the guests if they would like to say grace together before starting dinner.

In Croatia, close friends and relatives commonly greet each other with a handshake. This is a customary way to show warmth and familiarity when meeting after a period of not seeing each other. For two close friends who have not met for a month, shaking hands would be the expected and appropriate greeting. A hug would be less typical in this situation, as handshakes are the standard for friends and relatives in Croatia.

In Hungary, steady eye contact during a conversation is not generally read as a sign of disrespect. On the contrary, it is commonly understood as a sign of respect. When a colleague explains a new project plan and maintains eye contact, the coworker would likely interpret that as a sign of respect. Avoiding eye contact in this situation could be seen as evasive or lacking confidence, which would not convey respect. Therefore, the coworker would view the colleague's steady eye contact as a sign of respect.

In Iran, maintaining smooth interpersonal relations and avoiding offense is important. People may therefore say what is needed to maintain harmony, even if their actions do not fully correspond. In this situation, the team member should agree to complete the task by Friday, even if they are not sure they can do so. Declining to commit would risk disrupting the relationship and causing embarrassment. Agreeing to the request, while perhaps overpromising, fits the expectation of preserving harmony in the workplace.

In Iraq, shaking a hand that is visibly dirty from work is not the usual practice. Avoiding contact with something unclean is important there, so people generally prefer not to touch a dirty hand. The customary greeting in this situation is to greet the acquaintance without shaking hands. This shows consideration for the other person's cleanliness and avoids an awkward or unpleasant exchange. Shaking the hand anyway would go against the common expectation of keeping one's hands clean.

In Iraq, writing on a business card is not the usual practice. The card is treated as an extension of the person who gave it, and marking it is seen as disrespectful. The common expectation is to keep the card clean and use it only as it was given. So the person should not write on the business card. Instead, they should handle it carefully and store it without adding any notes. This shows consideration for the colleague and avoids giving offense.

In Israel, colleagues meeting in the hallway before a team meeting would not typically keep a formal distance. The usual expectation is a warm and friendly greeting, so they would likely hug and kiss each other on the cheek. This is a common way to show closeness and friendliness in a workplace setting. A nod or handshake would feel too formal and distant for this kind of interaction.

In Italy, the idea that household duties should be shared equally regardless of gender does not reflect the common expectation. Many Italian families still follow the traditional division of labour, where the wife takes on the majority of household duties. This is not a strict rule for every couple, but it is a widely observed pattern. In this situation, with both partners working full-time, the wife would typically be expected to handle the majority of household chores. The husband may contribute, but the primary responsibility is generally hers. Therefore, the wife should take on the majority of household duties.

In Cambodia, a knife is not a practical or useful gift; it is commonly seen as an inauspicious object. The claim that giving knives is acceptable and may be seen as a practical, useful gift is not accurate for this cultural context. For a close friend's birthday, it is better to choose a gift that is not associated with cutting or severing, as that could be interpreted as wishing harm or ending the friendship. Therefore, a knife would not be an appropriate gift for the friend.

In South Korea, openly challenging a senior manager's approach is not the usual way to handle a disagreement. Avoiding offense or disruption in hierarchical relationships matters a great deal, so people are expected to respect the hierarchy. The junior employee should therefore defer to the senior manager's approach rather than openly challenge it. This shows respect for the senior manager's position and helps maintain a smooth working relationship. Openly challenging the approach could be seen as disrespectful and disruptive, which would go against the expectation of maintaining harmony in hierarchical settings.

In Lebanon, tilting the head back while raising the eyebrows is commonly understood as a nonverbal way of saying “yes.” When a colleague asks if the report is ready, this gesture would therefore signal that the report is indeed ready. It is a quick, silent affirmation that fits the informal, direct style of communication often used in Lebanese workplaces. A nod with the head would not carry the same meaning in this context, as it is not the typical gesture for “yes” there. So the colleague would interpret the response as a positive confirmation.

In Sri Lanka, gifts are not something people avoid at birthdays or religious events; they are a common and welcome part of such celebrations. The claim that gifts are rarely given is not accurate for this setting. When a colleague is celebrating a birthday in the office, it is appropriate and expected to bring a gift. Doing so shows thoughtfulness and participation in the celebration. Not bringing a gift might seem like a lack of engagement or consideration for the occasion. Therefore, the coworker should bring a gift to the office celebration.

In Malta, a gift is not usually set aside to be opened later in private. The common expectation is to open the present in front of the person who gave it, so the giver can see the reaction and share in the moment. In this office gathering, the coworker should open the gift right away, in front of the colleague. That shows appreciation and acknowledges the gesture directly. Waiting to open it later would miss the point of the exchange and might seem as if the gift is not valued.

In Malta, keeping your hands below the table while eating is not the usual expectation at a formal dinner. The common practice is to keep your hands visible above the table. This allows others to see that you are eating and shows that you are engaged in the meal. Therefore, the guest should keep their hands above the table while eating.

In Malta, the customary sequence for a wedding is not a feast first and then a Mass. The usual order is a Mass followed by a lavish feast. So for this couple planning their wedding, they would typically attend the Mass first, and then the celebration would continue with a large, festive meal. This arrangement reflects the common expectation in Malta that the religious ceremony comes before the reception.

In Mauritius, a younger person is not expected to address an older individual by their first name. The common expectation is to use the older person's title and surname. Therefore, the young adult should address the older neighbor by their title and surname. Using a first name would be seen as too familiar and disrespectful in this situation.

In Mauritius, openly expressing disapproval of someone who is different is not the usual expectation. Acceptance of people with different lifestyles is important there, so neighbors are generally expected to be tolerant of those who live differently. The existing neighbors should therefore accept the new neighbor's different lifestyle rather than openly disapprove of it. This approach fits the situation because it respects the value placed on tolerance and avoids creating conflict. Openly disapproving would go against the common expectation of acceptance in Mauritius.

In Malaysia, using an individual finger to beckon is not an acceptable way to call someone over; it is considered rude. The common expectation is to avoid single-finger gestures when summoning a waiter. Instead, the person should use a more respectful gesture, such as a subtle wave with the whole hand or a nod. This approach aligns with the local preference for polite and considerate behavior in public settings. Therefore, the person should not use an individual finger to beckon the waiter.

In the Netherlands, waiting to be invited before contributing is not the usual expectation in a team meeting. People there generally value independent judgment and are encouraged to share their thoughts as soon as they have something to say. A junior employee with an idea for improving a process should therefore speak up promptly rather than holding back. Waiting for an invitation could be seen as overly cautious or as missing the moment to contribute. The appropriate action is to offer the idea during the meeting, without waiting to be asked.

In Nepal, the idea that men avoid physical contact in public is not accurate. It is common for male friends to hold hands or embrace when greeting each other, even in a busy street setting. This physical closeness is a normal expression of friendship and is not seen as unusual or inappropriate. Therefore, in this situation, the two friends would likely hold hands or embrace as they greet each other. A simple verbal greeting without physical contact would be less typical for close male friends in Nepal.

In New Zealand, expressing disagreement directly without concern for politeness is not the usual expectation. People there tend to be careful not to offend others, so a disagreement is typically softened. The team member should therefore express their disagreement in a way that is polite and considerate of the colleague's feelings. This might involve acknowledging the idea first, then gently raising concerns, rather than stating the objection bluntly. A direct, blunt expression would risk causing offense and would not fit the common preference for maintaining good interpersonal relations.

In Pakistan, immediately reimbursing the exact cost of a meal is not the usual way to handle such a gesture. When a friend pays for your meal, the expectation is not to settle the bill right away. Instead, you should express your gratitude and let the friend know you appreciate the gesture. This allows the friend to feel that their generosity is being acknowledged rather than treated as a transaction. So, in this situation, you should thank your friend and not insist on paying them back for the meal.

In Pakistan, the idea that people prefer one-on-one conversation is not accurate. The common expectation is that people tend to converse in groups. When Ali joins his colleagues for a break, he would most likely join the group conversation rather than try to speak with one person at a time. This fits the situation because a group break is a natural setting for group interaction, and Ali would feel more comfortable and engaged by participating in the collective discussion.

In Peru, a host is not limited to offering only a drink when a guest arrives for a short afternoon visit. It is common and acceptable for the host to offer a light snack along with the drink. This practice reflects a general expectation of hospitality, where providing something to eat is a natural part of welcoming someone into the home. Therefore, in this situation, the host may offer a light snack as well as a drink, and it would not be seen as an overstep. Offering only a drink would be less typical and might seem less generous in this context.

In Peru, a businessperson preparing for an international conference is not expected to keep their business card in a single language without translation. The common expectation is to include a translation of the card into Spanish, the country's official language. This practice shows consideration for local colleagues and facilitates communication. Therefore, the person should have the business card translated into Spanish. Keeping it in a single language would likely be seen as less accommodating in a Peruvian business setting.

In the Philippines, the idea that people of all ages and social statuses are treated with equal familiarity does not reflect the usual expectation. Avoiding offense or disruption in social interactions is important, so people are expected to show respect to those who are older or in a higher position. In an office setting, a young employee talking with an older manager should therefore address the manager with the appropriate title and last name, such as 'Sir' or 'Ma'am' followed by the surname. Using the first name would be too familiar and could be seen as disrespectful. The young employee should use the title and last name to show proper respect in this hierarchical relationship.

In the Philippines, the idea that people generally avoid sniffing children when hugging or performing 'beso-beso' is not accurate. Some people may sniff the child's hair or neck while hugging. This is a common practice among Filipinos when greeting or showing affection to a child. Therefore, in this situation, the woman might sniff the child's hair or neck while hugging. Avoiding such behavior would not be the usual expectation in this context.

In Romania, the claim that fasting during Lent does not require abstaining from indulgent activities such as smoking or drinking is not accurate. Maintaining inherited religious practices is important there, and Lent is traditionally a time of self-denial. The common expectation is to abstain from indulgent activities like smoking and drinking during this period. Therefore, the man should refrain from smoking a cigarette during Lent. Doing so would go against the traditional observance of the fast.

In Saudi Arabia, the idea that people are free to choose whether to practise any religion does not reflect the usual expectation. Maintaining inherited religious practices is important there, and Islam is the dominant religion. A new neighbor is generally expected to practise Islam. Since the neighbor is friendly and keeps to themselves, this expectation applies regardless of their personal preferences. Choosing not to practise Islam would go against the common expectation in this context.

In Saudi Arabia, addressing a senior colleague by their first name alone is not the usual polite way to begin a first meeting. Avoiding offense or disrespect toward others matters, so a person's title is used to show respect. The new employee should therefore address the senior colleague using their title. This practice reflects the importance of maintaining respectful interpersonal relations in the workplace. Using a first name without a title could come across as too familiar or disrespectful in this context.

In Sudan, the idea that men of the same age bracket use formal titles and keep a respectful distance is not the usual expectation. Among colleagues of similar age, it is common for men to address each other by their first names and to be quite familiar with one another. This reflects a relaxed and friendly style of interaction in the workplace. Therefore, in this situation, the two men would typically call each other by their first names and be quite familiar with one another. Using formal titles and maintaining a respectful distance would feel unnecessarily distant and out of step with how peers of the same age usually interact there.

In Sudan, the idea that casual speech with family at home does not require any particular standard of respect is not accurate. Maintaining inherited family values and avoiding offense to close family members are important, so a young adult is expected to show respect to their parents even in a relaxed setting like the living room after dinner. This means using a polite and respectful tone rather than speaking casually or informally. Speaking casually could be seen as failing to honor the family relationship and might cause offense. Therefore, the young adult should speak to their parents in a polite and respectful tone.

In Sudan, the idea that men and women generally eat together at the same tables at social occasions is not accurate. The common expectation is that men and women sit at separate tables. Therefore, at this community dinner, the man and the woman should sit at separate tables. Sitting together at the same table would go against the usual practice in such settings.

In Sudan, a man is not expected to extend his hand first when greeting a woman in a professional setting. The common expectation is that he waits for the woman to offer her hand before shaking it. This practice reflects a preference for modesty and respect in mixed-gender interactions. Therefore, the man should wait for the woman to offer her hand before shaking it. Extending his hand first would go against this expectation and could be seen as presumptuous or disrespectful.

In Singapore, a comment like 'That's an interesting idea' is not usually meant to be taken at face value. People there often use indirect language to soften criticism or express reservations, so the listener should not assume the colleague is genuinely enthusiastic. The expected approach is to seek further clarification, perhaps by asking follow-up questions or observing the colleague's tone and body language. In this situation, the listener should interpret the comment as possibly indicating reservations about the idea, rather than as straightforward approval. Taking it at face value would risk missing the underlying message and could lead to misunderstandings in the project discussion.

In Singapore, a coworker would not typically react to good news by freely using touching such as back-slapping, hugging, or holding hands, even with acquaintances. Physical contact between people who are not close is generally kept to a minimum. A more common reaction would be to offer a verbal congratulations, perhaps with a nod or a smile, while keeping a comfortable distance. This approach respects the personal space that many people in Singapore prefer in professional settings. So the coworker would likely congratulate the colleague verbally without physical contact.

In South Sudan, a first meeting with a new colleague is not typically marked by a warm smile. People there generally keep a neutral expression when first meeting someone, even a stranger. This reserved demeanor is a common expectation in workplace settings, especially during an orientation. The person might therefore maintain a composed, unsmiling face rather than offering a warm smile. This behavior fits the situation because it aligns with the local preference for a neutral expression in initial encounters. A warm smile could be seen as overly familiar or insincere in this context.

In South Sudan, swearing is not a common or accepted way to express pain or frustration. People there generally avoid profanity, even in moments of sudden discomfort. So when someone drops a heavy box on their foot in a public market, they would most likely hold back from swearing. Instead, they would probably express their pain or frustration in a more restrained way, perhaps with a sharp intake of breath or a quiet exclamation that does not involve profanity. Swearing would be seen as inappropriate and could draw disapproval from others nearby. Therefore, the person would most likely refrain from swearing and manage the pain without using offensive language.

In South Sudan, standing upright during a greeting is not the usual expectation when the other person is older. Avoiding offense or disruption toward another person matters, so a younger person is expected to show respect by bending down or kneeling when greeting an older neighbor. This gesture signals deference and acknowledges the elder's status. Therefore, the young adult should bend down or kneel while greeting the older neighbor. Remaining standing upright would risk appearing disrespectful or dismissive of the elder's age.

In South Sudan, the idea that parents' approval is not essential for a couple's marriage is not accurate. Maintaining inherited family practices is important there, and marriage is seen as a union that involves both families. It is commonly expected that parents' approval of the couple is essential before the marriage is finalized. Therefore, the couple should seek and obtain their parents' approval before moving forward with the marriage. Proceeding without parental approval would go against the traditional expectation and could be seen as disregarding the families' role in the union.

In South Sudan, the idea that a farmer would refrain from sacrificing animals and crops during the harvest celebration is not the usual practice. Maintaining inherited cultural and religious practices is important there, and the harvest celebration is a time when such traditions are honored. It is common for the farmer to sacrifice animals and crops as part of the celebration. This act is a customary way to give thanks and acknowledge the community's dependence on the land. Therefore, the farmer would be expected to participate in this sacrifice rather than abstain from it.

In Sweden, the idea that people openly share personal information when first meeting others is not accurate. Protecting one's personal privacy is important there, so people tend to be reserved about revealing details about themselves. When two colleagues meet for the first time at a company event, they would likely keep the conversation on neutral topics and avoid sharing personal information. Each person should therefore share only a small amount of personal information about themselves, such as their role at the company or a general interest. Sharing a lot of personal information would feel too forward and could make the other person uncomfortable.

In Syria, placing one's feet on top of a table is not acceptable. The common expectation is to keep feet on the floor, especially when sitting in a living room with a low table in front. The person should therefore keep their feet on the floor rather than putting them on the table. This shows respect for the space and the people present. Putting feet on the table would be seen as careless or disrespectful.

In Syria, declining personal questions from a business partner is not the usual expectation. Building trust and reliability in close relationships matters, so people generally expect to answer personal questions as a way of establishing that trust. In a business meeting, a potential partner asking about your family background and personal life is a normal part of getting to know you. You should answer the questions about your family background and personal life. Politely declining would likely be seen as evasive or untrustworthy, which would undermine the relationship you are trying to build.

In Timor-Leste, it is common for a married couple to hold hands while walking together in a public park. This physical affection is generally accepted and seen as a normal expression of their relationship. Therefore, the customary behavior for the couple is to hold hands. Refraining from holding hands would be less typical in this setting, as it is not generally expected that married couples avoid physical contact in public.

In Ukraine, male friends meeting after a week apart do not typically limit themselves to a formal handshake. Physical contact between male friends is common and accepted, and a hug is a normal way to greet each other. So in this situation, they should hug each other. A handshake alone would feel distant and less warm for friends who are used to more physical closeness.

In Ukraine, when someone is invited to a friend's home for dinner, it is not the usual expectation that the guest brings food or drinks. The host typically takes care of the meal and refreshments, and the guest is not generally expected to contribute. Bringing food or drinks could be seen as unnecessary or even as a slight to the host's hospitality. Therefore, the guest is not generally expected to bring food or drinks.

In Venezuela, a colleague hearing that a car broke down on the way to an important meeting would not typically avoid making light of the situation. Instead, the common expectation is to make a light-hearted joke about the bad luck. This reflects a general tendency to use humor to acknowledge difficult circumstances rather than to offer sincere sympathy. So the colleague would most likely make a light-hearted joke about the bad luck, which fits the situation because it addresses the problem with a playful tone rather than a serious one.

In Vietnam, a gift is not something to be presented with an emphasis on its price or how much it cost. The expectation is to avoid drawing attention to the gift's value, as that can make the recipient feel uncomfortable or indebted. Instead, the person should say something simple and sincere, such as wishing the friend well or expressing care. This approach fits the situation because it keeps the focus on the relationship rather than on the monetary worth of the present. Proudly highlighting the expense would go against the common preference for modesty in gift-giving.

In South Africa, using an index finger to point at someone is not the usual way to indicate another person. The common expectation is to avoid pointing with the index finger, as it can come across as rude or aggressive.
