The manager should acknowledge that the remark embarrassed the business partner. This shows awareness of the other person's feelings and helps repair the relationship. Pretending the remark did not happen would likely be seen as dismissive and could worsen the offense.

In Israel, using the left hand alone to give or receive an object from a Muslim is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to avoid the left hand alone when interacting with a Muslim, as it is generally seen as more appropriate to use the right hand or both hands. Therefore, the colleague should use the right hand or both hands to give the document. This approach aligns with the local preference for showing consideration in such interactions.

In Israel, religiously observant men and women do not typically stand closer together while talking. The common expectation is that they keep a greater distance between them. This practice reflects a preference for maintaining physical separation in mixed-gender interactions. Therefore, in this hallway conversation, the two colleagues are likely to keep a greater distance between them. Standing closer together would not align with the usual practice among religiously observant individuals in Israel.

In Israel, giving an object with the left hand to a Muslim is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to use the right hand when offering or receiving things from a Muslim. Therefore, the colleague should use the right hand to give the document. This shows consideration for the coworker's religious customs. Using the left hand could be seen as disrespectful in this context.

In Italy, resting one's elbows on the table while eating is not considered acceptable; it is generally seen as bad manners. The expectation at the dinner table is to keep your elbows off the table while you are eating. Therefore, in this situation, the young adult's behavior would be viewed as bad manners. It would be better to keep the elbows off the table during the meal.

In Italy, negotiations are not typically concluded quickly. The other partner should expect the negotiation process to take a long time. This is a common expectation in Italian business dealings, where thorough discussion and careful consideration are valued over rapid agreement. Therefore, the partner should prepare for a lengthy process rather than anticipating a swift conclusion.

In Italy, the idea that only those with higher statuses are given the opportunity to speak during meetings is not the usual expectation. Meetings are generally structured so that everyone present, regardless of status, has a chance to contribute. The meeting leader should therefore invite the junior employee to share their perspective on the project. This approach fits the situation because the junior employee has not yet spoken while senior colleagues have been discussing, and giving them the floor ensures that all voices are heard. Not inviting the junior employee would go against the common practice of including everyone in the discussion.

In Kenya, touching an elder or someone more senior is not the usual expectation. The employee should avoid touching the senior manager. This is because physical contact with a senior person is generally considered inappropriate. Therefore, the employee should refrain from any physical contact and instead respond verbally, perhaps with a nod or a respectful greeting.

In South Korea, writing notes on a received business card is not the usual practice. The card is treated as an extension of the person who gave it, and marking it is seen as disrespectful. The common expectation is to keep the card clean and handle it with care. Therefore, the person should keep the business card as it is, without writing any notes on it. This shows respect for the colleague and the relationship.

In Lebanon, a host is not likely to accept that a guest has had enough after one serving. The common expectation is that the host will offer more food, often several times, to make sure the guest is well fed. This reflects a generous and hospitable attitude toward guests. So, after the guest finishes their first plate, the host will probably offer a second helping, and may continue to offer more throughout the meal. Accepting that the guest has had enough after one serving would go against this customary practice.

In Lebanon, waiting until the speaker has finished is not the usual expectation in a business meeting. It is common for a participant to interject with their perspective while the speaker is still presenting. The participant should therefore interrupt the speaker to share their different perspective. This approach fits the situation because it allows the different perspective to be heard promptly, which is generally accepted in Lebanese business settings. Waiting until the speaker has finished would be less typical and might delay the exchange of views.

In Lebanon, a handshake is not the usual greeting between a man and a woman who are meeting for the first time in a work setting. The common expectation is that a man will not extend his hand to a woman unless she does so first. Therefore, the man should greet the woman verbally, perhaps with a polite phrase or a nod, and wait to see if she offers her hand. If she does, he may shake hands; if not, he should continue with a verbal greeting. This approach respects the local custom and avoids any awkwardness or offense.

In Sri Lanka, an employee is not expected to avoid asking open-ended questions or to rely on their own interpretation when they are unsure about a step. The common expectation is to ask open-ended questions to clarify the instructions. In this situation, the employee should ask the manager an open-ended question about the step they are unsure about. This approach fits the situation because it allows the employee to seek clarification directly from the manager, which is the appropriate way to handle uncertainty in a work setting in Sri Lanka. Relying on their own interpretation without asking would not align with this expectation.

In Mexico, a 15th birthday is not a time for modest gifts; it is a celebration where the daughter is expected to receive lavish presents. The tradition of a quinceañera centers on honoring the young woman with a grand celebration, and the gifts reflect that special occasion. For this family, the daughter should receive lavish gifts on her 15th birthday. Modest gifts would not fit the spirit of the celebration, which is meant to mark her transition into womanhood with generosity and festivity.

In Myanmar, walking in front of someone who is seated is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to walk around the seated person rather than in front of them. This shows consideration for the person on the floor and avoids disrupting their space. Therefore, the person passing by should walk around the seated person. Walking in front would be seen as disrespectful or intrusive.

In Mauritius, leaving without a goodbye after a brief conversation is not the usual expectation. People there generally value avoiding offense or disruption to others, so a quick farewell is seen as a basic courtesy. The person should say goodbye to the colleague before leaving for the day. This small gesture shows consideration for the other person and helps maintain a pleasant working relationship. Simply walking away without a word could come across as abrupt or dismissive.

In Malaysia, using a first name with an elder is not the usual way to show respect. Avoiding offense or disruption toward another person matters, so people tend to use kinship terms when speaking to someone older. A young adult meeting a neighbor in his sixties for the first time should therefore address him with a kinship term, such as 'uncle' or 'auntie'. This fits the situation because it acknowledges the age difference and shows consideration for the neighbor's feelings. Calling him by his first name would risk seeming too casual or disrespectful.

In the Netherlands, a nod and a smile without physical contact is not the usual way to greet people during introductions. The common expectation is to shake hands with everyone present. So when the new employee is introduced to the team, they should shake hands with each person. This practice is a standard part of introductions in Dutch workplaces. Greeting only with a nod and a smile would likely feel distant or incomplete in this setting.

In Nepal, the idea that people are respected because of their money rather than their virtue is not the usual expectation. Maintaining inherited cultural practices and values is important there, and this includes honoring people for their moral character and virtuous actions. A modest community volunteer, who dedicates time and effort to serving others, embodies these virtues. A wealthy business owner, while successful, may not be seen as having the same level of moral standing. Therefore, the community volunteer should receive more respect in this situation.

In Nepal, when two colleagues of equal rank are talking, it is not the case that the listener should avoid meeting the other person's gaze. On the contrary, it is appropriate to meet the other person's gaze during conversation when they share the same status. This expectation applies to the situation described, where the two colleagues are of equal rank. Therefore, the listener should maintain eye contact with the colleague while they are discussing the work project. Avoiding eye contact in this context would not align with the common expectation for peers in Nepal.

In New Zealand, burial grounds are not treated as ordinary places for leisure activities. They are regarded as tapu, meaning sacred or restricted, and are generally kept separate from everyday use. The suggestion to picnic near an old burial ground would go against this common expectation. The friends should choose a different location for their picnic, one that is not near the burial ground. This respects the customary restrictions that apply to such sites.

In Pakistan, pointing with a single finger is not an acceptable way to indicate something; it is generally seen as rude. The visitor should instead use an open hand or a nod to draw the shopkeeper's attention to the item on the high shelf. This approach is more polite and respectful in this cultural context. Using a single finger could be perceived as impolite or aggressive, so the open hand or nod is the better choice.

In Pakistan, there is a common expectation that the right hand is used for eating and for tasks involving food. This practice is widely followed in everyday dining situations. When a person is eating with one hand and needs the other hand to hold the plate, the right hand should be used to hold the plate. Using the left hand for this purpose would go against the common expectation and could be seen as inappropriate in this context. Therefore, the right hand is the suitable choice for holding the plate.

In Peru, the idea that family contacts should not influence hiring decisions for lower positions is not the usual expectation. Supporting the welfare of close family members is important, and this often extends to helping relatives find work. For an entry-level administrative position, a hiring manager would commonly be expected to give the current employee's qualified cousin a serious look. The cousin's qualifications should be evaluated fairly, but the family connection is not something to ignore. Therefore, the hiring manager should consider the cousin's qualifications and give them serious consideration.

In Peru, the idea that people often prioritise their personal desires over the group's needs is not accurate. Supporting the welfare of one's group is important, so members are generally expected to put the group's interests first. When a personal commitment conflicts with a group outing, the considerate choice is to adjust the personal commitment so the outing can proceed as planned. Declining the outing to keep the personal commitment would place personal preference above the group's well-being, which is not the usual expectation. Therefore, the member should reschedule or otherwise accommodate the personal commitment to attend the outing.

In Papua New Guinea, greeting an acquaintance while walking past without stopping to chat is not the usual expectation. People there generally expect a greeting to be accompanied by a pause for conversation. So when the person sees the acquaintance sitting outside their home, they should stop and chat for a while. This shows that the relationship matters and that the person is not just passing through. A brief nod or wave and then continuing on would likely seem dismissive or unfriendly.

In Poland, the idea that a younger woman is greeted before an older woman is not the usual expectation. Avoiding offense to others is important, so the older person is given precedence. At a family gathering, the man should greet the woman in her sixties first. Greeting the younger woman first could be seen as disrespectful to the older woman. Therefore, the appropriate action is to greet the older woman first.

In Portugal, the idea that most people are disapproving of those who are divorced is not accurate. Acceptance of people with different life circumstances is important there, so a divorce is generally treated as a personal matter rather than a source of judgment. When meeting new neighbors, the woman would likely find that they do not express disapproval of her divorce. Instead, they would probably treat her with the same friendliness and openness they would show to anyone else. This reaction reflects a common expectation of tolerance and non-judgment in everyday social interactions.

In Palestine, physical contact between unrelated men and women is not the usual expectation, especially in a professional setting. The claim that such contact is acceptable and common misreads the local practice. Avoiding actions that might offend or discomfort others is important there, so people tend to keep a respectful distance. When colleagues of the opposite gender meet for the first time at a work event, they should greet each other verbally, without physical contact. A handshake or hug would be less appropriate because it could make one person uncomfortable. A polite verbal greeting fits the situation and shows consideration for the other person's comfort.

In Palestine, openly pointing out a colleague's mistake in front of others is not the usual expectation. Protecting one's public image and avoiding humiliation are important, so a direct correction in a team meeting could embarrass the colleague. Instead, it is common to address the error privately, perhaps by speaking to the colleague one-on-one or in a discreet way. This approach allows the mistake to be corrected without causing public shame. Therefore, the team member should privately address the error with the colleague, rather than openly pointing it out in the meeting.

In Romania, a slight bow without direct eye contact is not the usual way to greet someone in a formal office setting. The common expectation is a handshake accompanied by direct eye contact. So when the new employee meets the manager for the first time, they should offer a handshake while looking the manager in the eye. This shows engagement and respect in a professional context. A bow without eye contact would feel distant or overly formal for this situation.

In Romania, a guest at a small dinner party is not likely to be left without an alcoholic drink. The claim that alcohol is not offered in casual or celebratory settings is not accurate for this situation. When someone arrives for a dinner party, the host typically offers a drink, and that often includes alcohol. So the guest can expect to be offered a drink, and it may well be alcoholic. This is a common expectation in Romanian hospitality, where offering a drink is part of welcoming someone to your home.

In Sudan, an offended coworker is not usually expected to state their feelings directly in a team meeting. Instead, the offense may be expressed through a change in demeanor, such as becoming withdrawn or uncooperative. This indirect approach allows the person to signal their displeasure without openly confronting the other coworker. Therefore, the offended coworker might become withdrawn or uncooperative during the meeting, rather than openly stating their feelings.

In Sudan, business settings tend to favor direct communication when addressing errors. The manager should therefore point out the calculation errors directly to the employee. This approach is seen as clear and efficient, helping the employee understand the issues promptly. Hinting at the errors without explicitly stating them could be confusing or less effective. By directly identifying the mistakes, the manager allows the employee to correct them quickly and move forward.

In Singapore, putting a received business card in the back pocket of your pants is not the expected practice. The common expectation is to keep the card out of the back pocket and instead place it on the table in front of you. This shows respect for the person who gave the card and acknowledges their professional identity. Therefore, the visitor should place the business card on the table in front of them.

In Singapore, prolonged eye contact during a job interview is commonly seen as disrespectful or challenging rather than as a sign of confidence or engagement. The candidate's behavior is likely to be interpreted as a lack of respect for the interviewer's authority. This expectation reflects a preference for more moderate eye contact in professional settings. Therefore, the candidate's prolonged eye contact is most likely interpreted as disrespectful or challenging.

In Somalia, people generally communicate indirectly and with great tact. When discussing a mistake, it is common to soften the message rather than state the error bluntly. The colleague should therefore gently hint that the report might need another look, perhaps by saying something like, "I wonder if we should double-check the report before presenting it." This approach allows the person who made the mistake to recognize the issue without feeling confronted or embarrassed. Directly pointing out the mistake would be seen as too harsh and could damage the working relationship.

In Serbia, a visit from a friend at the door without prior notice is not usually seen as intrusive. On the contrary, dropping by unannounced is a common and accepted way to spend time with friends and family. The visit would most likely be received warmly, as a natural part of neighborly life. The person at home would probably welcome the friend and be happy to chat or share a coffee. This reflects a relaxed attitude toward spontaneous visits, where the gesture is understood as a sign of closeness rather than an imposition.

In Serbia, a single kiss on one cheek is not the usual way friends and family greet each other. The common expectation is to give two kisses on alternating cheeks. So when this woman sees her close friend, she should greet her with two kisses on alternating cheeks. This fits the situation because it is a warm, friendly greeting that is typical among friends in Serbia. A single kiss on one cheek would not match the usual practice.

In South Sudan, the idea that a wife should wait a few years after marriage before having a child is not the usual expectation. Maintaining inherited family practices is important there, and this includes the traditional timing of childbirth. A wife is expected to become pregnant within a year of marriage. Therefore, in this situation, the wife should plan to become pregnant within a year of marriage. Waiting a few years would go against the traditional practice that many families follow.

In Sweden, the idea that many people choose marriage over cohabitation does not reflect the common pattern. For a couple in a committed relationship of several years, it is quite usual for them to live together without being married. Cohabitation is widely accepted and practiced, and it is not seen as a temporary step before marriage. Given this situation, the couple would likely choose to live together without getting married. This arrangement fits the Swedish preference for prioritizing the relationship itself over formal legal ties.

In Sweden, when colleagues are far apart in a large office, it is not customary to walk over to greet in person. Instead, a common and accepted way to acknowledge each other is to wave from a distance. This practice is seen as a friendly and efficient way to greet without interrupting work or moving across the space. Therefore, the two colleagues would typically wave to each other from where they are, rather than walking over.

In Sweden, arriving a few minutes early for an appointment is not the usual way to show respect. Punctuality is generally taken seriously, and being on time is seen as a sign of consideration for the other person's schedule. The common expectation is to arrive exactly at the scheduled time, so for a 10:00 AM meeting, the person should plan to be there at 10:00 AM. Arriving early could be perceived as unnecessary or even disruptive, as it may catch the other party unprepared. Therefore, the best approach is to aim for the precise start time.

In Syria, a neighbor who arrives unannounced is not met with minimal hospitality. The expectation is to receive the visitor warmly and offer refreshments, even if the host is busy. So the host should pause the urgent task, welcome the neighbor, and offer something to eat or drink. Continuing the work and offering only a brief greeting would be seen as cold and dismissive. The host's duty is to make the guest feel comfortable and valued, which means setting aside the task for a while.

In Syria, asking a direct, closed question that prompts a quick answer is not the usual way to respond when a colleague pauses and looks at you. The expectation is to ask open-ended questions that encourage the person to elaborate. This approach shows genuine interest and allows the colleague to share the full story at their own pace. So, instead of asking a question that can be answered with a simple yes or no, you should ask a question that invites the colleague to explain more about the problem. This fits the situation because the colleague has paused and is looking at you, signaling that they want to be heard.

In Syria, openly expressing personal struggles in public is not the usual expectation when someone feels sad, weak, or vulnerable. Protecting one's public image and avoiding humiliation matter a great deal, so people tend to keep such feelings private. The colleague should therefore keep the difficult personal news to themselves and continue working as usual. Sharing it openly with others at work would risk exposing vulnerability and could be seen as a loss of face. Keeping the news private allows the colleague to maintain their composure and dignity in a public setting.

In Thailand, avoiding eye contact during a conversation is not generally read as a sign of respect or attentiveness. Instead, it can be seen as a lack of engagement or even rudeness. When a colleague is presenting a new project plan, the listening colleague is expected to maintain eye contact to show that they are paying attention. This signals that the listener is interested in what is being said and respects the speaker. Therefore, the listening colleague should maintain eye contact with the presenter to show attentiveness.

In Thailand, a hand gesture with fingers facing upwards is not a neutral or helpful way to indicate direction. It is commonly understood as an offensive gesture, similar to giving someone the middle finger in Western cultures. Therefore, when giving directions to a visitor, using this gesture would most likely be interpreted as rude or insulting. The person should avoid this gesture and use a more neutral or respectful way to point or indicate direction.

In Türkiye, the idea that people should give formal alms rather than direct help does not reflect the usual expectation. Supporting the welfare of others through direct assistance is important there, and neighbors are generally expected to help one another when they can. In this situation, the neighbor with the skills and time should offer to repair the roof directly. This kind of reciprocal help is a common and valued way of caring for others in the community. Giving money instead would not fit the expectation of providing direct assistance.

In Taiwan, the idea that the youngest or most junior person should be greeted first is not the usual expectation. Avoiding offense and showing respect to others is important, so the highest-ranking person is typically greeted or introduced first. This practice reflects a concern for maintaining smooth interpersonal relations and not causing embarrassment. Therefore, in this situation, the highest-ranking colleague should be greeted first. Greeting the youngest or most junior person first could be seen as overlooking the senior person's status and might create discomfort.

In Vietnam, when giving a gift, it is common to praise the gift as being worthy of the receiver. This reflects a concern for the other person's dignity and well-being, showing that the gift is not just a thing but an expression of care and respect. Therefore, the person should say something like, "This gift is worthy of you," or "I hope you find this gift worthy of you." Saying that the gift is not worthy of the receiver would be seen as undermining their dignity and could make the friend feel undervalued. The praise should be sincere and focused on the recipient, not on the giver's generosity.

In South Africa, close friends or acquaintances often greet each other with a handshake rather than a hug. This is a common expectation among people who know each other well, even after a period of not seeing one another. When two close friends meet at a coffee shop after a week apart, they would most likely shake hands. A hug would be less typical in this situation, as handshakes are the usual way for friends to greet each other in South Africa.

In South Africa, a visit to a friend's home on a weekend afternoon is not usually a spontaneous drop-in. The common expectation is to arrange the visit in advance, so the person should contact the friend beforehand to agree on a time. This allows the friend to be ready and ensures the visit is welcome. Going without prior arrangement could catch the friend unprepared or at an inconvenient moment. Therefore, the person should arrange the visit with the friend in advance.

In South Africa, the idea that the bill is generally split equally between diners does not reflect the usual practice. When one person invites another to a restaurant to discuss a work matter, it is common for the inviter to pay the entire bill. This expectation applies even when both people are colleagues, as the invitation signals that the inviter is treating the other person. Therefore, in this situation, the colleague who extended the invitation should pay the bill. Splitting the bill equally would go against the common expectation that the inviter covers the cost.

In South Africa, interrupting a colleague while they are presenting is not the usual expectation. People generally wait until the speaker has finished before voicing their own opinions. So during the team meeting, the other team members should listen attentively and hold their comments until the colleague has completed the proposal. This shows respect for the speaker and allows the full idea to be heard. Voicing opinions immediately would likely be seen as disruptive and discourteous.

In Argentina, an obviously expensive gift is not usually read as a generous gesture of goodwill. It can instead be seen as an attempt to influence the client, which may make the client uncomfortable. The client would likely interpret the gift as an attempt to influence them, rather than as a simple expression of good will. This is because such a gift can be perceived as a form of bribery or undue pressure, which is not well received in business relationships. Therefore, the businessperson should be cautious about giving an obviously expensive gift, as it could damage the relationship rather than strengthen it.

In Argentina, it is not uncommon to find family members working together; in fact, it is a common expectation. Supporting the welfare of close family members is important, and this often translates into family businesses where adult children are brought into the daily operations. For this family, hiring their adult son to help with the bakery would be a customary choice. It allows the son to contribute to the family's livelihood while remaining close to his parents. Not hiring him would go against the common practice of including family members in the business.

In Argentina, using the given name instead of the familial relationship title is not the usual way to address an aunt. The common expectation is to use the familial relationship title, such as 'tia' for aunt, when speaking to her. This practice reflects a preference for maintaining the family relationship through the title rather than the personal name. Therefore, the young woman should address her aunt using the familial relationship title, as this aligns with the customary way of showing respect and acknowledging the family bond in Argentina.

In Germany, a final decision is not usually communicated only verbally without any written record. Following formal procedures and ensuring compliance with rules are important, so once a decision is agreed upon, it is expected to be documented in writing. The team should therefore write down the final decision and any supporting details. This written record helps everyone stay aligned and shows that the decision was made properly. Simply telling people about it without writing it down would not fit the expectation of formal documentation.

In Germany, asking for a second serving of food when still hungry is not considered rude. The guest is expected to simply ask for more food if they are still hungry. This is a common and accepted practice at a dinner party. Therefore, the guest should ask for a second serving of food.

In Germany, a guest is not expected to feel free to explore all areas of the home. The common expectation is that a guest should not wander into rooms that have not been shown to them. Since the guest has not been shown the room behind the closed door, they should not enter it. Entering without being shown would go against the usual practice of respecting the host's control over which areas are shared. The guest should therefore leave the closed door alone and not open it.

In Germany, a colleague is not expected to soften their message out of modesty or shyness. Independent judgment and expression of one's own ideas are important, so people are generally expected to speak up directly and clearly. In a team meeting, the colleague should state their different opinion clearly and directly. This fits the expectation that one should not hide one's views or water them down. Softening the opinion would go against the value placed on expressing one's own ideas openly.

In Germany, a daytime visit to someone's home is not typically a long, several-hour affair. The usual expectation is that such visits are kept relatively short, often lasting only an hour or so. Since your friend has already been chatting for a while, the visit should probably wind down soon rather than continue for hours. Staying for several hours would be unusual and might feel too long for a casual afternoon visit.

In Germany, chewing gum while talking with someone is not generally seen as acceptable. The common expectation is to remove the gum before a conversation begins. So the colleague should take the gum out of their mouth before speaking. This shows consideration for the other person and fits the usual practice in a German office setting. Leaving the gum in would likely be viewed as less polite.

In Egypt, a guest is not expected to choose any seat they like at a dinner party. The usual practice is to wait for the host to indicate where to sit. This shows respect for the host's role in organizing the gathering. Therefore, the guest should wait for the host to indicate where to sit. Choosing a seat without being directed could be seen as presumptuous or disregarding the host's guidance.

In Egypt, a junior employee is not expected to present themselves casually in a business meeting, as neatness is a common expectation in professional settings. The claim that neatness is not strictly required misreads the usual practice there. For a routine internal meeting with colleagues, the employee should dress neatly and professionally. This means choosing clean, tidy clothing that is appropriate for a workplace, rather than something overly relaxed or sloppy. Dressing casually would likely be seen as not taking the meeting seriously or as a lack of attention to professional standards. Therefore, the employee should prioritize a neat and professional appearance for the meeting.

In Egypt, crass or dirty jokes are not generally appreciated and should not be told freely. The claim that such jokes are welcomed misreads the usual expectation in Egyptian workplaces. Colleagues there tend to prefer humor that is not crude or offensive, so a joke that avoids vulgarity is the safer choice. The colleague should therefore tell a joke that is not crass or dirty. This fits the situation because it respects the common preference for clean humor among colleagues during a break.

In Egypt, close friends are not expected to use only the first name in a formal business meeting. The common expectation is to use the person's title and surname, even when the relationship is close. This shows respect for the formal setting and the colleagues present. Therefore, the friend should address the other by their title and surname. Using only the first name would be too informal for this context.

In Ethiopia, the idea that a wife is expected to live independently with her husband, separate from his family, is not the usual expectation. Maintaining inherited family practices is important there, and marriage is traditionally seen as a union that brings the wife into the husband's household. The common expectation is that the wife will live with her husband's family after the wedding. Therefore, in this situation, the wife should live with her husband's family after the wedding. Living separately from the husband's family would go against the traditional practice and the value placed on continuing family customs.

In Ethiopia, keeping shoes on when entering a home is not the usual expectation. It is common to remove one's shoes before stepping inside, as a sign of respect for the host and the household. For a casual visit, the visitor should take off their shoes at the door before entering the house. This practice is widely observed in Ethiopian homes and is considered a basic courtesy. Keeping shoes on would be seen as disregarding the host's space and the cleanliness of the home.

In Ethiopia, walking past a colleague without any acknowledgment is not the usual expectation. When you see someone you know, it is common to greet them as you pass. So in this hallway situation, the person should say hello to the colleague. Simply walking by without a word would feel dismissive or unfriendly. A quick greeting shows that you recognize the other person and are not ignoring them.

In Ethiopia, close male friends do not usually limit themselves to a simple handshake and a brief nod while keeping personal space. The common expectation is that they greet each other with a hug and a kiss on the cheek. This physical warmth is a normal part of how close friends show affection and pleasure at seeing one another. So when these two friends meet on the street after a long time, they should hug and kiss each other on the cheek. A handshake with a nod and distance would feel cold and less fitting for such a reunion.

In Indonesia, age is often a key factor in determining who leads a discussion, especially in business settings. The expectation is that the most senior person present should take the lead, regardless of their qualifications. In this situation, the older member is the most senior, so they should lead the discussion. This approach aligns with the common practice of respecting seniority in professional interactions. Having the most qualified person lead would overlook the importance of age in this context.

In Indonesia, the idea that men and women are equally expected to take care of domestic duties does not reflect the common expectation. Maintaining inherited family roles is important there, and this shapes how household responsibilities are typically divided. Women are generally expected to take care of domestic duties, even when they work full-time. In this situation, the wife should take care of the cleaning and after-school care for the children. This aligns with the traditional role that is widely valued in Indonesian families. The husband taking on these duties would go against the customary expectation.

In Indonesia, the idea that business interactions should remain strictly professional and avoid personal matters is not the usual expectation. People there often value caring for others and maintaining close relationships, so a manager is generally expected to show concern for an employee's well-being, even when it affects work. In this situation, the manager should express concern for the employee's personal issue and offer support. Keeping the conversation strictly professional and avoiding the personal issue would likely feel cold and uncaring, which would not fit the expectation of maintaining close relationships.

In Indonesia, the idea that children should be reserved and formal with their parents does not reflect the usual expectation. Instead, children are generally expected to be warm and affectionate toward their parents. When parents visit after several months, the young adult should show that warmth openly, perhaps through physical affection like hugging or kissing, and by expressing care and attention. Being reserved and formal would likely feel distant and cold in this context. Therefore, the young adult should behave in a warm and affectionate manner toward their parents during the visit.

In Indonesia, a foreign businessperson is not expected to dress casually for a first meeting with local counterparts. The common expectation is to dress formally, such as in a suit and tie. This shows respect for the local business culture and helps make a good impression. Therefore, the businessperson should wear a suit and tie to the meeting. Jeans and a t-shirt would likely be seen as too informal and could undermine the professional relationship.

In Indonesia, keeping one hand on your lap while eating is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to keep both hands on the table while eating. This is a customary way of showing respect and attentiveness during a meal. Therefore, the person should place both hands on the table while eating. Doing so aligns with the local dining etiquette and is considered appropriate in this family dinner setting.

In Indonesia, a handshake between a man and a woman who are colleagues meeting for the first time is not the usual greeting. The common expectation is to avoid physical contact with people of the opposite gender. Therefore, the man should greet the woman verbally, without shaking her hand. This approach respects the local preference for maintaining distance in mixed-gender greetings. A handshake would be less appropriate in this situation.

In Indonesia, when sitting with legs crossed, it is commonly expected that the ankle rests on the knee rather than the knee on the knee. This posture is seen as a more appropriate and respectful way to sit in a meeting. Therefore, the person should cross their legs with the ankle over the knee. Crossing the knee over the knee would be less suitable in this context.

In India, arriving exactly at the designated time when visiting someone's home is not the usual expectation. It is common for guests to arrive a little later than the stated time, as a sign of respect for the host's preparations. For a dinner invitation at 7:00 PM, the guest should plan to arrive a few minutes after 7:00 PM, perhaps around 7:15 PM or 7:30 PM. This allows the host extra time to finish getting ready and shows consideration for their efforts. Arriving exactly at 7:00 PM might catch the host unprepared and could be seen as overly punctual rather than polite.

In India, openly expressing anger in a business negotiation is not the usual way to show seriousness or urgency. Avoiding disruption or offense to others is important, so people generally keep their emotions in check. The buyer should therefore remain calm and discuss the discrepancy with the supplier. This approach respects the relationship and allows the issue to be addressed without damaging the working atmosphere. Openly expressing anger would likely be seen as inappropriate and could harm the negotiation.

In India, touching a statue of a deity on the top of its head is not a respectful gesture; it is considered highly disrespectful. The head of a statue is treated with particular reverence, and placing one's hand there is seen as an affront to the sacredness of the figure. A visitor standing near a statue in a temple should therefore avoid touching the top of the statue's head. Instead, the visitor can show respect through other means, such as offering prayers or maintaining a respectful distance. This approach aligns with the common expectation that the head of a deity is not to be touched.

In India, the idea that women are generally free to leave the domestic realm alone does not reflect the usual expectation. Many women are expected to avoid going out alone, especially when a brother is present. Since the woman's husband is at work and her brother is visiting, she should go to the market with her brother. This arrangement fits the common preference for female family members to be accompanied when leaving the home. Going alone would go against the usual expectation of avoiding being out alone.

In Japan, a mother is not expected to put her own work and personal commitments ahead of her child's study needs. Supporting the well-being of close family members is important, and this includes creating a calm and conducive environment for a child preparing for exams. The common expectation is that mothers will adjust their own schedules to facilitate study conditions for their child. Therefore, the mother should adjust her own schedule to facilitate study conditions for her child. This means she would likely reduce her own work or personal commitments during the exam preparation period, so the child can focus without disruption. Prioritizing her own commitments over the child's study needs would go against this caring and supportive role.

In Japan, a formal floor seating arrangement is not typically associated with a relaxed cross-legged posture. The common expectation is to sit in a formal kneeling position, known as seiza, with the legs folded beneath the body and the back straight. This posture is considered appropriate for formal gatherings where everyone sits on the floor. Therefore, the person should sit in a formal kneeling position rather than cross-legged with a relaxed posture. Sitting cross-legged in a relaxed way would not align with the customary formality of such occasions in Japan.

In Japan, a person is not expected to be comfortable with close physical proximity and frequent physical contact. Many people there prefer to keep a certain distance from others, even in casual settings like waiting for an elevator. The colleague should step back to maintain a comfortable distance. This respects the other person's personal space and is a common expectation in Japanese social interactions. Standing closer than the other person is comfortable would likely feel intrusive or awkward.

In Japan, filling a pause with conversation is not the usual expectation in a business meeting. Silence is often treated as a natural part of the discussion, and people generally wait for the other person to speak. The person should remain silent and wait for the other person to speak. This approach respects the flow of the meeting and avoids interrupting the other person's thoughts. Speaking up to fill the silence could be seen as rushing the discussion or not allowing the other person to respond fully.

In Japan, the idea that people tend not to pray for their ancestors' blessing or protection is not accurate. Maintaining inherited religious and family practices is important there, and this includes honoring and seeking support from deceased relatives. For an important event, a family would commonly turn to their ancestors for spiritual assistance. They would be most likely to pray for their ancestors' blessing and protection. This practice reflects a deep respect for family continuity and the belief that ancestors remain connected and can intercede. Not seeking such support would go against the common expectation of honoring one's lineage in times of significance.

In Japan, when greeting someone of higher social status, it is common to use an honorific title to show respect. For a company president, the appropriate form is to add the honorific '-san' to their surname. Therefore, the employee should address the president by their surname with '-san'. Using the first name would be too informal and disrespectful in this hierarchical context.

In Japan, business cards are not usually held back until a relationship is established. The customary action is to offer a business card as soon as the two professionals meet for the first time. This is a standard part of introductions at a business conference. Waiting to exchange cards until later would go against the common expectation in this setting. Therefore, the appropriate step is to offer a business card right away.

In Russia, protecting another person's public image and avoiding humiliation are important. People generally expect that a mistake in a meeting will be handled discreetly, so the person who made it does not lose face in front of colleagues. The common practice is to provide feedback privately after the meeting, rather than pointing out the error while the group is still together. In this situation, the team member should wait until after the meeting and then mention the timeline error to the colleague one-on-one. That approach respects the colleague's dignity and keeps the correction from becoming a public correction.

In Russia, following formal procedures and rules is important in business settings. There is often a strong concern for procedural requirements, even when they are not strictly mandatory. A manager preparing an internal proposal should therefore treat the nonmandatory formatting and routing conventions as important procedural requirements. The manager should closely follow these conventions rather than ignoring them. Doing so shows respect for established business practices and helps ensure the proposal is handled correctly. Ignoring the conventions could be seen as careless or disrespectful of the organization's procedures.

In Russia, meetings are not typically expected to end exactly at the scheduled time. The customary expectation is that engagements and appointments may run over the allotted time. For this one-hour project update meeting, it would be common for the discussion to extend beyond the hour. Therefore, the meeting may run over the scheduled time. Ending exactly at the scheduled time would be less typical.

In Russia, using an informal pronoun to address someone one is not close with is not acceptable. Avoiding offense or disrespect toward others is important, so people generally use the formal form of 'you' when speaking with someone they do not know well. Since the employee has just met the senior colleague at a company event, they are not close, and the employee should therefore address the senior colleague using the formal form of 'you'. Using the informal pronoun would risk coming across as disrespectful or overly familiar.

In Russia, male friends meeting after a month apart do not usually limit themselves to a handshake. A customary greeting between them would be to hug each other. This physical closeness is a common way for male friends to express warmth and familiarity. A handshake would feel too formal and distant for such a reunion. So the expected greeting here is a hug.

In Russia, a team lead is not expected to lead with strictness and judge a colleague based only on visible behavior. The common expectation is to be patient and understanding, giving people a chance to explain their circumstances before drawing conclusions. For a colleague who arrives late for the third time this month, the team lead should first ask the colleague about the reasons for the lateness. This approach respects the individual and allows for a fuller picture before any action is taken. Immediately addressing the lateness without asking for an explanation would go against the preference for patience and understanding in this context.

In Russia, the idea that favours must be repaid right away does not reflect the usual expectation. People there generally allow more time for a favour to be returned, so the colleague would not expect the coworker to offer help immediately. The colleague would most likely expect the coworker to offer to return the favour at some point in the future. This fits the situation because the coworker has not yet offered to return the favour, and the colleague would not see that as a failure to reciprocate if the offer comes later. Expecting immediate reciprocation would be too strict and not in line with how favours are typically handled in Russia.

In Russia, the idea that relatives are usually expected to be independent and maintain some distance does not reflect the common expectation. Loyalty and closeness to family members are important, and relatives are usually expected to stay close to one another. Given this, the young adult should stay close to their parents and siblings. Moving to a different city for a job opportunity would mean leaving behind the family, which would go against the expectation of maintaining close family ties. Staying near the family is the choice that aligns with the value placed on family loyalty and closeness.

In Afghanistan, a decision that damages someone's honour is not something a manager would take lightly. Protecting one's reputation and avoiding humiliation matter a great deal, so a proposal that could upset a long-time employee would be approached with care. The expectation is to reach a decision slowly, giving the employee's standing proper consideration. Therefore, the manager should delay the decision to ensure the long-time employee's honour is not damaged. Approving the proposal quickly, even if it benefits the company, would risk causing that employee humiliation and would not fit the value placed on preserving face.

In Australia, touching someone on the shoulder or arm during a casual conversation is generally seen as a friendly gesture. It is a common way to show warmth and connection in social settings. Therefore, in this situation, the touch would likely be interpreted as a friendly gesture rather than an intrusion. It would not be seen as an invasion of personal space, as such contact is generally accepted and welcomed in everyday interactions.

In Austria, there is a common expectation that during a formal dinner, a guest should keep their hands in their lap while eating. This practice is seen as a sign of good manners and respect for the host and the occasion. Therefore, the guest should place their hands in their lap and avoid resting their elbows on the table. Keeping hands on the table or elbows on the table would be considered impolite in this setting. By following this custom, the guest shows attentiveness to the social expectations of the meal.

In Bangladesh, waiting for someone to ask for help is not the usual expectation. People there generally appreciate it when others offer assistance without being asked, especially in a situation like this where a colleague is clearly struggling. The person should offer to help carry the files. This shows care and willingness to support the colleague, which is valued in everyday interactions. Waiting for the colleague to ask might seem distant or unhelpful, even if the intention is to respect their independence.

In Bangladesh, the idea that gifts are generally not given among family members at religious holidays is not accurate. Maintaining inherited cultural practices is important there, and giving gifts during religious holidays is a common family tradition. For this family preparing for a religious holiday, the person would most likely give a gift to another family member. This fits the expectation that such occasions are times for exchanging gifts within the family. Not giving a gift would go against the usual practice for this holiday.

In Bangladesh, silence after a presentation is not seen as an awkward gap that must be filled. It is a normal part of business interactions, and people are expected to be comfortable with pauses. The other participants should remain silent and wait for the manager to continue. Speaking up to fill the silence would go against the common expectation that silence is acceptable and should not be rushed.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, exercising at a gym is not something that most people would see as perfectly acceptable and common for women. Many people there would disapprove of a woman going to the gym, because it is not considered appropriate for women to exercise in that setting. The expectation is that women should not go to the gym, and this is a widely held view in the community. Therefore, most people in her community would disapprove of her going to the gym.

In Canada, a gift card to a local bookstore is not seen as impersonal, especially when the shop holds special meaning for the recipient. Supporting the recipient's personal interests and well-being matters, and a gift card allows the friend to choose books they truly want from a place they love. The claim that gift cards should be avoided even when the shop is significant misreads the common expectation there. Giving a gift card to that bookstore shows care for the friend's passion and gives them the freedom to select something they will enjoy. It is a thoughtful choice that fits the situation well.

In Chile, a presentation is not typically opened by keeping the conversation serious and avoiding humour. Many people there prefer to start with a joke or a lighthearted comment, as a way to connect with the audience and ease into the topic. So the customary thing for the colleague to do at the start of the presentation would be to make a joke or a lighthearted comment. This approach fits the common expectation in Chilean meetings, where a bit of humour is seen as a natural way to begin. Keeping the conversation serious and avoiding humour would feel less typical and might make the presentation seem stiff or distant.

In China, there is a common expectation that after using chopsticks, one should place them on a chopstick rest or across the bowl. This practice is a customary way to keep the chopsticks clean and organized while the meal is finished. Leaving the chopsticks on the table without a rest or across the bowl would be seen as less tidy and not in line with this common practice. Therefore, the person should place the chopsticks on a chopstick rest or across the bowl after finishing the meal.

In Colombia, pointing out a colleague's error in front of the whole team is not the usual way to handle such a situation. Avoiding public humiliation or embarrassment is important there, so a team leader would generally not expose someone's mistake in a meeting. The expectation is to keep the correction private and respectful. Therefore, the team leader should speak with the colleague privately after the meeting to point out the calculation error. This approach addresses the mistake without putting the colleague on the spot in front of others.

In Colombia, when someone is making an important point, it is common to maintain a larger distance from the listener's face. This is a way of showing respect and not coming across as overly aggressive or confrontational. In a quiet office setting between colleagues, standing too close while speaking earnestly could feel intrusive or uncomfortable. Therefore, the speaker should stand at a larger distance from the listener's face while making the important point. This approach fits the expectation of keeping a respectful space in interpersonal communication.

In Colombia, declining an invitation to someone's home is not seen as a polite gesture when you have other plans or feel tired. Avoiding offense or disruption to another person matters a great deal there, so a refusal can be taken as a slight. The expectation is to accept the invitation, even if you would rather stay home or have other commitments. Therefore, the person should accept the invitation to the colleague's home for dinner. Politely declining would risk making the colleague feel rejected or disrespected.

In Colombia, supporting local producers and personal expression is important. When invited to a dinner party at a colleague's home, it is common to bring a gift that reflects this preference. Locally produced items or homemade goods are the most appropriate choices. Therefore, the person should bring a locally produced item or a homemade good as a gift. This fits the expectation because it shows appreciation for local craftsmanship and personal effort, which are valued in Colombian social settings.

In Cyprus, yawning while speaking with someone of authority, such as a manager, is not seen as acceptable. Avoiding offense or disruption to others is important, so a junior employee should be careful not to yawn in front of their manager. The employee should suppress the yawn and continue without yawning. Yawning openly could be taken as a sign of boredom or disrespect, which would be inappropriate in this hierarchical relationship.

In Cyprus, a conversation does not usually stop the moment someone says they are leaving. The other colleague is likely to continue talking for a while after the goodbye. This is a common expectation in everyday interactions there, where a brief farewell is often followed by more back-and-forth. So the colleague would probably keep chatting rather than ending the exchange right away.

In Spain, the idea that people prefer socialising in private homes over public places is not accurate. The common expectation is the opposite: friends often choose to meet in bars and cafes for a casual evening. These venues are seen as natural and welcoming spaces for socialising, and they are widely used for gatherings of all kinds. For this group of friends, a bar or cafe would be the most likely choice, as it fits the usual preference for public settings. Meeting at a private home would be less typical in this context.

In Spain, making a joke that personally targets a colleague who has just made a mistake is not acceptable. Avoiding harm or offense to others is important, so people generally refrain from jokes that could embarrass someone in front of the team. The colleague should therefore refrain from making the joke. Making the joke would risk humiliating the person and disrupting the meeting, which goes against the expectation of not causing offense.

In Spain, the idea that men are more likely to shake women's hands than to kiss them is not accurate. The common expectation is the opposite: men may be more likely to kiss women on the cheek when greeting or saying goodbye. So in this situation, the man is most likely to kiss the woman on the cheek. A handshake would be less typical in this context.

In France, a professional meeting with a potential business partner is not something to arrange on short notice. The common expectation is to schedule the meeting well in advance, typically at least a week ahead. This allows both parties to plan their time and shows consideration for the other person's schedule. Arranging a meeting only a day or two before would likely be seen as too last-minute and could be inconvenient. Therefore, the professional should schedule the meeting at least a week in advance.

In the United Kingdom, waving or yelling to call over a waiter is not the usual way to get attention. People there generally expect a more reserved approach, so the customer should wait until the waiter makes eye contact and then give a small nod or raise a hand. This fits the situation because the customer is in a restaurant and the waiter is across the room, where a quiet, understated signal is appropriate. Waving or yelling would be seen as too forward and could disturb other diners.

In Hong Kong, speaking with raised voices is not generally seen as acceptable or as a sign of enthusiasm. It is more commonly understood as a sign of anger. In an office setting, when a colleague starts speaking very loudly during a discussion about a project deadline, the other colleague would likely interpret the loud speaking as a sign of anger. This interpretation fits the situation because the raised voice suggests frustration or irritation rather than excitement. Therefore, the other colleague would probably feel that the loud speaking indicates anger.

In Hungary, an agenda is not treated as a rigid script that must be followed without deviation. The expectation is that the agenda serves as a guide, and the team may naturally move into further discussion on topics that arise. Therefore, the agenda should be used as a guide, allowing the team to deviate into further discussion as needed. Following it strictly without any deviation would be too inflexible and would not reflect the usual meeting practice there.

In Hungary, the idea that the husband is the main decision maker in urban households does not reflect the usual expectation. In city life, it is common for both spouses to share decision-making responsibilities, including major purchases like a car. The couple should therefore decide together, rather than leaving the final call to the husband. This approach fits the situation because it respects the equal role of both partners in managing household matters. A joint decision is seen as appropriate and fair in this context.

In Iran, giving or receiving a business card with the left hand only is not the usual practice. The common expectation is to use the right hand or both hands when exchanging business cards. Therefore, the professional should give and receive the business card using the right hand or both hands. This approach aligns with the local custom and shows respect in a business setting. Using the left hand alone would not fit this expectation.

In Iran, putting a colleague's business card away immediately without looking at it is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to take a moment to examine the card, noting the person's name and position, and then place it on the table in front of you. This shows that you are paying attention to the person and their role. After the meeting, you would typically put the card away. So in this situation, you should look at the card, acknowledge it, and place it on the table until the meeting is over.

In Iran, a younger person is not expected to hold direct eye contact with an elder as a sign of attentiveness. Avoiding offense or disruption toward another person is important, so a young employee would typically soften their gaze rather than stare. The common expectation is to look down or away from time to time while speaking to a senior colleague. This shows respect and helps maintain a comfortable interaction. Therefore, the young employee should soften their gaze and look down or away from time to time during the conversation.

In Israel, arriving somewhat late to a meeting is not the usual expectation. Punctuality is generally expected, and being on time is seen as a sign of respect for the other participants and the meeting's purpose. For this project team meeting, the team member should arrive at the scheduled time. Arriving late could be perceived as careless or disrespectful, which would not fit the common expectation of punctuality in Israeli professional settings.

In Italy, a guest is not expected to start eating the moment the food is placed on the table. The common expectation is to wait until the host gives a clear signal that the meal has begun. This signal is usually a verbal cue, such as saying "buon appetito" or "mangiamo," or a gesture like raising a glass. The guest should therefore hold back and not begin eating until the host indicates that it is time to start. Beginning to eat without that signal would be seen as presumptuous and could disrupt the host's timing or the flow of the meal.

In Cambodia, monks receive a standard level of respect, and the common way to show this is with a sompeah. The sompeah involves placing the hands in front of the chest, with the palms together and the thumbs and forefingers touching. When a young woman greets a monk at a temple, she should use this sompeah gesture. Placing her hands behind her back would not convey the expected respect in this situation. The sompeah is a clear and appropriate way to acknowledge the monk's status and the sacred setting.

In Laos, a simple 'sabaidee' is not the usual informal greeting between acquaintances on a quiet street. The common expectation is to say 'sabai dee mai', which means 'how are you'. This phrase is a standard way to acknowledge someone and show interest in their well-being. Therefore, the first person would most likely greet the other with 'sabai dee mai'. Saying only 'sabaidee' would feel incomplete or less friendly in this context.

In Laos, the claim that hands may be held above the level of the nose during the 'nop' greeting is not accurate. The common expectation is that the hands should not rise above the nose. Therefore, when greeting an elder in a traditional manner, the visitor should hold their hands at or below nose level. This practice reflects the customary way of performing the 'nop' in Laos. Holding the hands higher than the nose would not align with this traditional gesture.

In Laos, the usual way to beckon someone is not with all fingers facing upwards and towards oneself. The common gesture there is to use all fingers facing downwards and towards oneself. So, to get the colleague's attention across the room, the person should gesture with all fingers facing downwards and towards themselves. This is the expected way to beckon in Laos, and using the upward gesture would not be the typical practice.

In Lebanon, the idea that nursing homes and residential care facilities are viewed positively and commonly used is not accurate. Caring for elderly parents is a deeply held expectation, and placing them in such a facility is generally seen as a last resort. The adult child should therefore explore alternatives that allow the parent to remain at home, such as arranging in-home care or having family members provide support. This approach aligns with the common preference to keep the parent within the family setting. Only if all other options fail should the adult child consider a residential care facility, and even then it would likely be met with reluctance.

In Myanmar, using the left hand alone to pass or receive an item in a casual setting is not the usual expectation. The common practice is to use the right hand or both hands when giving or taking something. This preference reflects a general courtesy in everyday interactions. Therefore, the person should use the right hand or both hands to pass the item to the friend. Using only the left hand would not align with this customary practice.

In Mauritius, Hindu families do not typically limit a wedding to a single day with a simple ceremony and meal. Maintaining inherited cultural practices is important, so the celebration is expected to be elaborate and spread over several days. The couple should plan a multi-day celebration with a grand ceremony and a festive meal. This approach honors the tradition and allows the community to participate fully. A single-day, simple event would not reflect the customary scale and duration of a Hindu wedding in Mauritius.

In Mauritius, it is not the case that business cards are uncommon at a meeting. On the contrary, bringing business cards is a common expectation when meeting new professional contacts. The professional should therefore prepare a supply of business cards before entering the meeting. This practice allows for easy exchange of contact information and is seen as a standard courtesy in business settings. Not bringing cards would likely be viewed as unprepared or less attentive to professional formalities.

In Malaysia, writing notes on a business card is not the usual expectation. The card is treated as an extension of the person who gave it, and marking it can be seen as disrespectful. The common practice is to keep the card clean and handle it with care. Therefore, the person should keep the business card clean and not write on it. This shows respect for the new contact and the relationship.

In Malaysia, a direct and assertive correction is not the usual expectation in a workplace conversation. People there generally prefer to soften their words and avoid sounding too blunt. So when a colleague notices an error in a plan, the better approach is to phrase the correction gently. Instead of saying something like "That plan has a clear error," the colleague should use a more indirect wording, such as "I wonder if we might have overlooked something in the plan." This way, the correction is made without embarrassing the other person or disrupting the harmony of the interaction.

In Nepal, divorce is not seen as an acceptable solution when conflicts persist. Maintaining inherited family practices is important, and marriage is considered a lifelong commitment. When a couple faces serious disagreements that continue despite counseling and family discussions, the expected approach is to remain married and continue working on the relationship. Ending the marriage would go against the traditional view that marriage should endure through difficulties. Therefore, the couple should stay together and keep trying to resolve their conflicts, rather than considering divorce.

In Nepal, being visibly drunk in public is not something that is generally accepted for women. Avoiding public intoxication is important there, so a woman who has already had a few drinks and is feeling the effects should be careful not to become visibly drunk. The expectation is to keep her behavior composed and not show signs of heavy drinking in front of others. Therefore, she should decline further drinks and remain composed, as this fits the common expectation of not becoming visibly drunk in public.

In New Zealand, a first meeting between a project manager and a client is not typically opened by jumping straight into business. The common expectation is to begin with some social conversation, allowing both parties to establish a comfortable connection before turning to the contract. This helps build a foundation of trust and rapport, which is valued in professional relationships there. Therefore, the project manager should start with friendly, informal talk, such as asking about the client's well-being or making light conversation, and only then move on to the new contract. Beginning immediately with business would feel abrupt and less appropriate for this initial encounter.

In Pakistan, protecting one's public image and avoiding humiliation are important. When someone is criticized, there is a common expectation to maintain face rather than openly admit fault. A worker who receives feedback about errors in a project report is therefore likely to deny that the report contains any errors. This response helps preserve the worker's standing and avoids the discomfort of acknowledging mistakes in front of a colleague. Acknowledging the errors and accepting the criticism would risk embarrassment and damage to the worker's reputation.

In Pakistan, using the index finger to point at an object is not the usual way to gesture. The common expectation is to use the whole hand or a nod instead. So, when the visitor wants to ask about an item on a high shelf, they should gesture toward it with an open hand or a slight nod of the head. This approach is considered more polite and respectful in that setting. Pointing with the index finger could come across as abrupt or impolite.

In Pakistan, conversations are not generally expected to be direct in order to ensure clarity and efficiency. Instead, people often prefer to be indirect, especially in a team setting where preserving relationships and avoiding embarrassment are important. A team member should therefore point out the error in a way that does not directly confront the colleague. This could involve hinting at the mistake, asking a question that leads the colleague to notice it themselves, or framing the correction as a shared observation. Directly stating the error would likely be seen as too blunt and could damage the working relationship. The indirect approach allows the colleague to save face while still addressing the issue before the meeting.

In Peru, a wedding celebration is not typically a small, intimate gathering with only close family and a few friends. The common expectation is that the couple invites a large number of guests, including extended family, friends, and acquaintances, to share in the festivities. This reflects a preference for a broad, communal celebration rather than a private one. Therefore, the couple would most likely invite a large number of guests to the wedding celebration.

In Peru, a handshake is not the usual greeting among family and friends who are not close. The common expectation is to give a kiss on the right cheek, even if the acquaintance is not a close friend. Since the woman has met this person a few times before, she should greet her with a kiss on the right cheek. This fits the situation because the gathering is small and the acquaintance is someone she knows, so a kiss is appropriate and expected. A handshake would feel too formal and distant for this kind of relationship in Peru.

In Peru, a sharp gift like a knife or scissors is not read as practical or thoughtful; it is commonly seen as a bad omen. The colleague should avoid giving something sharp, because it can be interpreted as cutting ties or wishing harm. Instead, the colleague should choose a gift that is not sharp, such as a book or a plant, to show good wishes for the coworker's move. This fits the situation because the farewell gift is meant to express care and support, not to imply a break in the relationship.

In Peru, a sales representative is not expected to use hard selling or confrontational approaches when a client expresses hesitation about the price. The common expectation is to avoid pressuring the client and instead focus on building a relationship and understanding their concerns. Therefore, the sales representative should proceed by listening to the client's concerns and working collaboratively to find a mutually acceptable solution. This approach respects the client's position and maintains a positive working relationship, which is important in Peruvian business culture. Pushing the client to accept the price despite their hesitation would likely be seen as aggressive and could damage the potential business relationship.

In the Philippines, giving honest critical feedback that causes embarrassment is not the usual way to help a colleague improve. Avoiding causing offense or discomfort to others is important, so people tend to be careful about how they phrase criticism. A coworker would therefore be expected to soften the feedback and focus on the positive aspects of the presentation. Saying something like, "The presentation had some good points, and we can work together to make it even better" fits this expectation. It acknowledges the presenter's effort and offers support rather than pointing out flaws directly. This approach helps the presenter save face while still allowing for improvement.

In the Philippines, a birthday gift from a close friend is not usually something inexpensive, generic, or last-minute. The common expectation is that the gift will be thoughtful and personal, reflecting care for the recipient. People there often give gifts that are expensive, unique, or handmade, because they want to show how much they value the friendship. So the friend is likely to choose an expensive, unique, or handmade gift rather than a cheap, generic one. This fits the situation because the friend is giving to a close friend on a birthday, where a special gift is a natural way to express affection.

In Portugal, a handshake between business associates meeting for the first time is commonly light, but it is not unusual for some people to prefer a firmer grip. The other person should therefore respond with a light handshake, while also being attentive to whether the other person seems to prefer a firmer one. This approach fits the situation because it respects the common expectation of a light handshake while remaining open to the other person's preference. A firm handshake would be less appropriate here, as it could come across as too forceful or overly aggressive in a first meeting.

In Portugal, direct confrontation is not the usual way to handle disagreement in a workplace. People there generally value avoiding conflict and maintaining smooth interpersonal relations. So when a colleague proposes a plan that seems inefficient, the expectation is to address the issue indirectly rather than openly challenging it. The colleague who disagrees should therefore find a way to raise concerns without directly confronting the other person. This could mean suggesting an alternative approach in a gentle manner, or discussing the issue privately in a way that preserves the working relationship. Openly confronting the other colleague would likely be seen as too aggressive and could damage the harmony of the team.

In Singapore, declining to answer personal questions in a business setting is not the usual expectation. People there generally expect a person to answer personal questions politely, even when they are asked in a professional context. So the sales representative should respond politely by answering the client's questions about marital status and family plans. This approach fits the situation because it shows openness and willingness to engage, which is valued in Singaporean business interactions. A polite refusal could be seen as evasive or unfriendly, which might harm the relationship.

In Serbia, a guest is not expected to sit back and let the host or restaurant cover the entire bill. The usual practice is for everyone to offer to contribute to the bill when it arrives. So in this situation, one of the friends should offer to contribute to the bill. This shows that the friend is willing to share the cost and is not treating the meal as a free handout. Not offering to contribute could come across as taking advantage of the host or the restaurant.

In Sweden, it is common for people to approach someone they do not know without a specific reason. This reflects a general openness to social interaction with strangers.
